standards.pe_text: Construct an explanation based on evidence for how the structure of DNA determines the structure of proteins, which carry out the essential functions of life through systems of specialized cells.

stimuli.title: A Change of One Letter
stimuli.phenomenon: Hemoglobin is the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. The instructions for building hemoglobin are stored in a gene — a section of DNA. In some people, a single change in that DNA changes one of the building blocks (amino acids) in the hemoglobin protein. That one change makes the hemoglobin protein behave differently: the altered hemoglobin sticks together into stiff rods when oxygen is low, pulling the normally round red blood cell into a curved “sickle” shape. Sickled cells are stiff, break down faster, and can jam narrow blood vessels. The blood smear below shows crescent-shaped sickle cells among normal round cells. In the questions that follow, you will use this example to explain how the structure of DNA determines the structure and function of a protein.

figure.caption: Figure 1. A blood smear from a person with sickle cell disease: stiff, crescent-shaped sickle cells among round, normal red blood cells. (Image: Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

questions.stem: Put the events in order (1 = first) to show how one DNA change leads to a sickled red blood cell.
items: The whole hemoglobin protein changes shape and clumps into stiff rods.
One building block (amino acid) in the hemoglobin protein is changed.
A single change occurs in the DNA of the hemoglobin gene.
The red blood cell is pulled into a stiff sickle shape.
questions.rationale: DNA change → amino-acid change → protein-shape change → cell-shape change (C → B → A → D).

questions.stem: The sickle cells are a different shape because—
options: the red blood cells were built with the wrong number of chromosomes.
a change in the DNA changed the shape of the hemoglobin protein, and a protein's shape determines what it does.
the sickle cells are missing their DNA, so they cannot hold their shape.
the cells ran out of oxygen and shrank permanently on their own.
questions.rationale: DNA sets the protein's structure and structure determines function; A/C/D miss the DNA→protein link.

questions.stem: Select all statements the sickle-cell example supports about DNA, proteins, and traits.
options: A protein's job depends on its shape, so a change in shape can change how it works.
Changing the DNA can never affect a protein.
The order of the instructions in DNA determines the structure of a protein.
A trait such as cell shape can be traced back to the instructions stored in DNA.
Red blood cells build hemoglobin with no connection to DNA.
questions.rationale: A, C, D state the DNA→protein→trait principle; B and E are the misconceptions.

questions.stem: Predict: if a different DNA change did not disrupt the hemoglobin protein, the red blood cells would most likely—
options: still sickle, because DNA does not affect protein shape.
keep their normal round shape and carry oxygen normally.
lose their DNA and stop working.
become a completely different type of cell.
questions.rationale: Task demand 3 — predict the effect of a DNA change on protein structure/function; normal protein shape → normal cell shape and function.

stimuli.title: Insulin With The Wrong Shape
stimuli.phenomenon: Insulin is a protein that acts as a signal. After a meal, insulin normally attaches to a matching site on the body's cells and tells them to take glucose (sugar) out of the blood. The instructions for building insulin are stored in a gene, a section of DNA, which sets the order of the protein's building blocks called amino acids. In some people, a single change in the insulin gene changes one amino acid, so the insulin protein folds into a different shape. Because its shape no longer fits the matching site on the cells, the altered insulin cannot signal them to take in glucose, and glucose builds up in the blood. The graph compares blood glucose in a person with typical insulin and a person with altered insulin, before and after a meal. In the questions that follow, you will use this example to explain how the structure of DNA determines the structure and function of a protein.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Blood glucose for a person with typical insulin and a person with altered insulin.
figure.title: Blood Glucose Before and After a Meal

questions.stem: The graph shows blood glucose for a person with typical insulin and a person with altered insulin. Which statement best describes the data?
options: The two people have about the same blood glucose at all times.
The person with altered insulin has much higher blood glucose, especially after a meal.
The person with altered insulin has lower blood glucose after a meal.
Blood glucose is highest for the person with typical insulin.
questions.rationale: The altered-insulin bars are far higher, and the gap is largest two hours after the meal, when working insulin should have cleared glucose from the blood. Choosing 'about the same' or 'lower' misreads the height of the bars.

questions.stem: Use the information to complete the cause-and-effect chain. A change in the insulin [Drop-down 1] changes one amino acid, so the insulin protein folds into a different [Drop-down 2]. Because its new shape no longer fits the matching site on body cells, the cells are not signaled to take in glucose, and the amount of glucose in the blood [Drop-down 3].
dd: gene | number of chromosomes | cell type
stays high | drops below normal | is not affected
questions.rationale: A change in the DNA (gene) changes an amino acid, which changes the protein's shape, and a protein's shape sets its job; a poorly fitting insulin cannot clear glucose, so glucose stays high. Picking 'chromosome number' or 'color' breaks the DNA-to-shape link.

questions.stem: Decide whether each statement is True or False based on the insulin example.
rows: The example supports the idea that a change in DNA can change how well a protein works.
A protein's shape helps determine the job it can do.
The altered insulin fails to work because the person's cells contain no DNA.
Changing the DNA instructions for insulin had no effect on the insulin protein.
questions.rationale: The first two statements restate the DNA -> shape -> function principle the data support. The false statements express the misconceptions that specialized cells lose their DNA and that changing DNA cannot affect a protein.

questions.stem: Choose the word or phrase that makes each prediction correct.
items: If a different DNA change did NOT alter insulin's shape, the insulin would [ still / no longer ] fit the matching site on cells.
In that case, the cells would be signaled to take in glucose, so blood glucose would stay [ in the normal range / very high ].
This shows that a protein's job depends on its [ shape / DNA location ].
questions.rationale: A DNA change that leaves the protein's shape unchanged leaves its function unchanged, so glucose is cleared normally. Choosing 'very high' would treat every DNA change as harmful, ignoring that only shape-changing changes disrupt the protein.

stimuli.title: An Enzyme For Pigment
stimuli.phenomenon: Melanin is the brown pigment that gives color to a person's skin, hair, and eyes. Melanin is built by a protein called an enzyme. The instructions for building this enzyme are stored in a gene, a section of DNA that sets the order of the enzyme's building blocks, called amino acids. This order folds the enzyme into a specific shape that lets it do its job. In some people, a single change in the gene changes one amino acid, so the enzyme folds into a shape that cannot build melanin. With little or no working enzyme, very little pigment is made, and the person has very pale skin and hair and light-sensitive eyes. The table shows how the typical and altered enzymes compare. In the questions that follow, you will use this example to explain how the structure of DNA determines the structure and function of a protein.

figure.caption: Table 1. How a change in the pigment-enzyme gene affects the amount of pigment (melanin).

questions.stem: According to the table, how does the altered enzyme differ from the typical enzyme?
options: It has a changed DNA instruction and a misshapen form, so it cannot build melanin.
It has more chromosomes than the typical enzyme.
It builds the same amount of pigment as the typical enzyme.
It contains no DNA at all.
questions.rationale: The altered row differs in the DNA instruction and the enzyme shape, and its 'Can it build melanin?' entry is 'No.' The distractors invent a chromosome difference or ignore the 'Very little' pigment result shown in the table.

questions.stem: Match each observed change to the level it describes.
rows: A single instruction in the DNA is changed
One building block (amino acid) of the enzyme is different
The enzyme is folded into a form that cannot work
The skin and hair have very little color
questions.optset: change in the DNA / change in an amino acid / change in the protein's shape / change in the trait
questions.rationale: The chain runs from a change in the DNA, to a changed amino acid, to a changed protein shape, to a changed trait. Mismatches show the levels of the DNA -> protein -> trait relationship have been confused.

questions.stem: Arrange the steps in order (1 = first) to construct the explanation of how one DNA change leads to pale skin and hair.
items: One amino acid in the enzyme is changed.
Very little melanin is made, so the skin and hair are very pale.
A change occurs in the DNA of the pigment-enzyme gene.
The enzyme folds into a shape that cannot build melanin.
questions.rationale: DNA change -> amino-acid change -> protein-shape change -> trait change. Placing the pale-color result or the shape change before the DNA change breaks the cause-and-effect order.

questions.stem: Complete the prediction. Suppose a different change in the gene did not change the enzyme's shape. The enzyme would [Drop-down 1] be able to build melanin, so the amount of pigment would be [Drop-down 2]. This shows that what a protein does depends on its [Drop-down 3].
questions.rationale: If the shape is unchanged, the enzyme keeps its function and pigment stays normal, because a protein's job depends on its shape. Choosing 'no longer' or 'very low' would treat any DNA change as disabling regardless of its effect on shape.

standards.pe_text: Develop and use a model to illustrate the hierarchical organization of interacting systems that provide specific functions within multicellular organisms.

stimuli.title: Muscles Under Pressure
stimuli.phenomenon: A high school soccer player wears a fitness monitor during practice. While she stretches at the side of the field, the monitor shows a slow, steady heart rate and calm breathing. As the coach moves the team through walking, then jogging, then full-speed running, she notices that her heart begins to pound and she breathes much harder and faster. Within seconds of stopping, both her heart rate and breathing slow back down. Her working leg muscles need extra oxygen to stay active, and that oxygen must be pulled into the body and carried to the muscles quickly. No single organ does this alone. Instead, several body systems adjust together so the muscles get what they need. The chart shows how her heart rate and breathing rate changed as her activity increased. In the questions that follow, you will use the data to model how different body systems interact to support her muscles during exercise.

figure.caption: Figure 1. One player's heart rate and breathing rate at increasing activity levels.
figure.title: Heart Rate and Breathing Rate During Activity

questions.stem: The chart shows the player's heart rate and breathing rate as her activity increased. Which statement best describes the relationship between the two?
options: As activity increases, heart rate rises but breathing rate stays the same.
As activity increases, both heart rate and breathing rate rise together.
As activity increases, both heart rate and breathing rate fall.
Heart rate and breathing rate change in opposite directions.
questions.rationale: Both curves climb from rest to running, showing the circulatory and respiratory responses rise together to meet the muscles' demand. Choosing an 'opposite' or 'unchanged' option misreads the coordinated increase shown in the data.

questions.stem: Complete the flow of events during exercise. When a person exercises, the [Drop-down 1] system senses the activity and speeds up the heartbeat. The heart is part of the [Drop-down 2] system, which carries oxygen taken in by the [Drop-down 3] system to the working muscles.
questions.rationale: The nervous system signals the heart, the circulatory system transports oxygen-rich blood, and the respiratory system brings oxygen into the body; together they supply the muscle system. Distractors name systems not involved in delivering oxygen to muscles.

questions.stem: Match each structure to the body system it belongs to.
questions.optset: circulatory / respiratory / nervous / muscle
questions.rationale: Each organ-level structure is a component of a larger system in the body's hierarchy. Mismatches reveal confusion about which level of organization performs which function during activity.

questions.stem: Select all that apply. If the player's circulatory system could not increase blood flow during exercise, which effects would be expected?
options: The working muscles would receive less oxygen than they need.
The muscles could not keep up their increased activity for long.
The digestive system would immediately shut down.
The person would tire more quickly.
Breathing rate would no longer be connected to the muscles' needs.
questions.rationale: Removing the circulatory system's ability to deliver more blood starves the muscles of oxygen, limiting activity and causing fatigue. The unselected options describe effects that do not follow from this single change.

stimuli.title: From Meal To Cells
stimuli.phenomenon: After a student eats a sandwich and drinks a glass of milk, several organs work together to process the meal and deliver its nutrients to the body. In the mouth, the food is broken into smaller pieces and moistened. It then passes to the stomach, which churns it into a thick liquid. Next, in the small intestine, the food is broken down further and its nutrients are absorbed into the blood. From there, the blood vessels of the circulatory system carry the nutrients to cells all over the body, where they are used for energy and growth. No single organ does this alone; the digestive and circulatory systems must work together. The table lists the organs involved and what each one does. In the questions that follow, you will build and use a model to explain how structures in two body systems interact to process a meal and deliver its nutrients.

figure.caption: Table 1. Organs that work together to process a meal and deliver its nutrients.
columns: Main job in handling the meal
rows: Breaks food into smaller pieces and moistens it
Churns the food into a thick liquid
Finishes breaking down food and absorbs nutrients into the blood
Carry the absorbed nutrients to cells throughout the body
Absorbs water and packs the remaining waste

questions.stem: According to the table, which organ absorbs the meal's nutrients into the blood?
options: The mouth
The stomach
The small intestine
The blood vessels
questions.rationale: The table lists 'absorbs nutrients into the blood' as the job of the small intestine. The mouth and stomach only break food down, and the blood vessels carry nutrients after they are already absorbed.

questions.stem: Arrange the steps in order (1 = first) to build a flow chart tracing a nutrient from the meal to a body cell.
items: In the small intestine, nutrients are absorbed into the blood.
In the mouth, food is broken into smaller pieces.
Blood vessels carry the nutrients to cells throughout the body.
In the stomach, the food is churned into a thick liquid.
questions.rationale: The path is mouth -> stomach -> small intestine -> blood vessels -> body cells, showing the digestive and circulatory systems handing off in turn. Placing absorption or transport before chewing and churning breaks the order of the interacting systems.

questions.stem: Match each structure from the digestive system to its level in the body's organization.
rows: A single muscle cell in the stomach wall
The layer of muscle tissue in the stomach wall
questions.optset: cell / tissue / organ / organ system
questions.rationale: Cells make up tissues, tissues make up organs, and organs make up organ systems, showing the hierarchical organization of the body. Mismatches reveal confusion about which level a structure belongs to.

questions.stem: Decide whether each statement is True or False. Suppose the small intestine could no longer absorb nutrients into the blood.
rows: Body cells would not receive the nutrients from the meal.
The circulatory system would have fewer nutrients to deliver.
Digestion in the mouth would immediately stop.
The person could still get the meal's nutrients to their cells as usual.
questions.rationale: Blocking absorption cuts the hand-off from the digestive to the circulatory system, so cells go without nutrients and the blood has little to deliver. Chewing in the mouth is upstream and would continue, so the third statement is false and the last contradicts the disruption.

stimuli.title: The Working Artery Wall
stimuli.phenomenon: An artery is a blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart. Each heartbeat pushes a surge of blood into the arteries under high pressure. The wall of a large artery contains two important tissues: a layer of stretchy elastic tissue and a layer of smooth muscle. The elastic tissue lets the artery stretch as blood surges in and spring back between beats, smoothing out the flow. The smooth muscle can tighten or relax to make the artery narrower or wider, changing how much blood reaches the tissues beyond. Signals from the nervous system tell the smooth muscle when to tighten or relax, so more blood can be sent to the legs during running. The graph shows blood flow to the leg muscles when the arteries work normally and when they are too stiff to widen. In the questions that follow, you will use a model to explain how two body systems interact to deliver the right amount of blood.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Blood flow to the leg muscles at rest and during running, for healthy arteries and for stiff arteries that cannot widen.
figure.title: Blood Flow to Leg Muscles

questions.stem: According to the graph, how does blood flow to the leg muscles change from rest to running in a person with healthy arteries?
options: It increases greatly.
It decreases greatly.
It stays about the same.
It drops to zero.
questions.rationale: The healthy-arteries bar rises from 100 at rest to 300 during running as the vessels widen to deliver more blood. The distractors contradict the clear increase shown by the bars.

questions.stem: Complete the description of how the artery works. In an artery wall, the [Drop-down 1] lets the vessel stretch as blood surges in and spring back between beats. The [Drop-down 2] can tighten or relax to change how wide the artery is. The signals telling it to tighten or relax come from the [Drop-down 3] system.
dd: elastic tissue | bone tissue | nerve tissue
questions.rationale: The elastic tissue provides stretch and recoil, the smooth muscle changes the vessel's width, and the nervous system supplies the signal, so the circulatory and nervous systems work together. The distractors name tissues or systems that do not perform these jobs in the artery wall.

questions.stem: Choose the word or phrase that makes each statement correct.
items: The elastic tissue smooths out the blood flow because it can [ stretch and spring back / stay stiff ].
To send more blood to the legs, the smooth muscle makes the artery [ wider / longer ].
To adjust blood flow, the circulatory system works together with the [ nervous / digestive ] system.
questions.rationale: Stretch and recoil even out the surges, widening the vessel raises flow to the legs, and the nervous system provides the control signal. Choosing 'stay stiff,' 'longer,' or 'digestive' misses how each component's property supports the shared function.

questions.stem: Select all that apply. What would be expected if the smooth muscle in the leg arteries could no longer relax to widen the vessels?
options: Less extra blood would reach the leg muscles during running.
The leg muscles would tire more quickly during exercise.
The arteries could not adjust blood flow to match the body's activity.
The bones in the legs would stop growing.
The lungs would no longer take in any air.
questions.rationale: The stiff-arteries bar shows running flow reaching only 150 instead of 300, so the muscles get less blood, tire sooner, and flow can no longer track activity. Bone growth and breathing are not controlled by this artery function, so those options do not follow.

standards.pe_text: Plan and conduct an investigation to provide evidence that feedback mechanisms maintain homeostasis.

stimuli.title: Steady After The Sugar
stimuli.phenomenon: A patient at a clinic eats a meal containing bread, fruit, and juice. A continuous monitor records the concentration of glucose (sugar) in her blood every 30 minutes for three hours. Before the meal, her blood glucose sits near a steady level that her body normally keeps fairly constant, called a set point. Soon after she eats, the glucose concentration climbs well above that level. Rather than continuing to rise, it peaks and then drops back down, returning close to the original set point by the end of the three hours. Her body senses the change and responds: the pancreas, a gland, releases a hormone that helps lower the amount of glucose in her blood. The graph shows how her blood glucose concentration changed over time. In the questions that follow, you will use the data to explain how a feedback mechanism keeps her blood glucose near a stable set point.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Blood glucose concentration measured every 30 minutes after a meal.
figure.title: Blood Glucose After a Meal

questions.stem: The graph shows the patient's blood glucose concentration after eating. Which statement best describes what happened?
options: Glucose stayed constant the whole time.
Glucose rose after the meal and then returned toward its starting level.
Glucose fell after the meal and kept falling.
Glucose rose after the meal and stayed at the high level.
questions.rationale: The curve spikes after the meal and then settles back near 90 mg/dL, the pattern of a system disturbed and then returned to its set point. Selecting 'stayed high' or 'kept falling' ignores the return that signals homeostasis.

questions.stem: Choose the word that makes each statement about the feedback mechanism correct.
items: When blood glucose rises above the set point, the pancreas releases [ more / less ] hormone.
In response, the blood glucose concentration [ falls / rises ] back toward the set point.
This kind of feedback [ opposes / increases ] the original change to keep the internal environment stable.
questions.rationale: Negative feedback responds to a disturbance by acting against it: a rise triggers a hormone that lowers the concentration back toward the set point. Picking 'increases' would describe a runaway change rather than maintenance of a steady state.

questions.stem: Arrange the steps of the feedback mechanism in the order they occur, starting with the disturbance.
items: The pancreas releases a hormone that lowers blood glucose.
After a meal, blood glucose rises above the set point.
Blood glucose returns to its stable set point.
The pancreas detects the high glucose level.
questions.rationale: The causal chain runs: disturbance (glucose rises), detection, hormone response, return to set point. Ordering the response before the detection breaks the cause-and-effect logic of the feedback loop.

questions.stem: Decide whether each statement about the investigation and its data is True or False.
rows: To show that homeostasis was maintained, measurements had to continue until glucose returned to its stable set point.
A single glucose reading taken right after the meal would be enough to show that the feedback mechanism worked.
Recording glucose at several times lets you see both the disturbance and the return to the set point.
Because glucose returned near its starting level, the data provide evidence that a feedback mechanism kept the internal environment stable.
questions.rationale: Evidence for homeostasis requires data showing the return to equilibrium, so repeated measurements are needed and a single early reading is insufficient. Recognizing the false statement shows students can evaluate the sufficiency of the collected data.

stimuli.title: Holding A Steady Temperature
stimuli.phenomenon: The human body keeps its internal temperature near a steady set point of about 37 degrees C (98.6 degrees F). Researchers recorded how a volunteer's body responded as the surrounding air changed. When the person stepped into a hot room, the body temperature began to rise above the set point. In response, the body increased sweating, and as the sweat evaporated it carried heat away, cooling the body back toward 37 degrees C. Later, in a cold room, the body temperature began to fall below the set point. This time the person began to shiver, and the rapid muscle movements released heat that warmed the body back toward 37 degrees C. In both cases the body sensed a change from the set point and responded in a way that returned the temperature to normal. The table summarizes these responses. In the questions that follow, you will use the data to explain how a feedback mechanism keeps body temperature near a steady set point.

figure.caption: Table 1. The body's responses to temperature changes around its set point of about 37 degrees C.
rows: Evaporation removes heat; temperature falls toward 37 degrees C
Muscle activity releases heat; temperature rises toward 37 degrees C

questions.stem: According to the table, what does the body do when it becomes too hot?
options: It shivers, which releases heat and raises the temperature.
It sweats, and the evaporation removes heat and lowers the temperature toward the set point.
It stops responding until the temperature returns on its own.
It raises the set point to match the hot room.
questions.rationale: The hot-room row lists increased sweating, with evaporation removing heat and lowering the temperature toward 37 degrees C. Shivering is the cold-room response, and the body defends its set point rather than changing it.

questions.stem: Match each item to how it relates to the body's temperature set point.
questions.optset: cools the body when it is too hot / warms the body when it is too cold / the steady temperature the body maintains
correct: cools the body when it is too hot
warms the body when it is too cold
the steady temperature the body maintains
questions.rationale: Sweating cools, shivering warms, and the set point is the steady value the responses return the body to. Mismatching the two responses shows the directions of the feedback have been reversed.

questions.stem: Complete the causal chain for a cold room. When the air is cold, the body temperature falls [Drop-down 1] the set point. The body senses this change and responds by [Drop-down 2]. This response [Drop-down 3] the body temperature back toward the set point.
dd: raises | lowers | has no effect on
questions.rationale: A cold room drops the temperature below the set point, shivering is the response, and it raises the temperature back toward normal, acting against the disturbance. Choosing 'sweating' or 'lowers' would drive the temperature further from the set point.

questions.stem: Select all that apply. Which measurements would give the best evidence that the body returned to its temperature set point after being too hot?
options: Recording body temperature at several times until it returns to about 37 degrees C.
Noting when sweating starts and when it stops.
Measuring body temperature only once, at the moment the person feels hottest.
Comparing the final body temperature with the set point.
Recording the person's shoe size.
questions.rationale: Evidence of a return to homeostasis requires repeated temperature readings, a record of the response (sweating), and a comparison of the final value with the set point. A single reading at the peak cannot show a return, and shoe size is irrelevant.

stimuli.title: Breathing Keeps Carbon Dioxide Steady
stimuli.phenomenon: The body keeps the amount of carbon dioxide (CO2) in the blood near a steady set point. Carbon dioxide is a waste gas released by the body's cells; the blood carries it to the lungs to be breathed out. When CO2 builds up and rises above the set point, sensors detect the change, and the body responds by increasing the breathing rate. Breathing faster and deeper removes CO2 from the blood more quickly, bringing it back toward the set point. When blood CO2 drops below the set point, breathing slows, letting CO2 build back up to normal. In this way the breathing rate constantly adjusts to keep blood CO2 stable. The graph shows a volunteer's blood CO2 and breathing rate over time after CO2 was raised above the set point of about 40 units. In the questions that follow, you will use the data to explain how a feedback mechanism keeps blood CO2 near a steady set point.

figure.caption: Figure 1. A volunteer's blood CO2 and breathing rate over time after blood CO2 was raised above the set point.
figure.title: Blood CO2 and Breathing Rate Over Time

questions.stem: According to the graph, what happened to the breathing rate as blood CO2 rose above the set point?
options: The breathing rate increased.
The breathing rate decreased.
The breathing rate stayed the same.
The blood CO2 never changed.
questions.rationale: As the CO2 line climbs above 40, the breathing-rate line rises from 12 to about 30 breaths per minute. The other options contradict the upward breathing-rate curve or the clear rise in CO2.

questions.stem: Complete the causal chain. When blood CO2 rises [Drop-down 1] the set point, the body responds by making the breathing rate [Drop-down 2]. Faster, deeper breathing removes CO2 from the blood, so the blood CO2 [Drop-down 3] the set point.
dd: returns toward | rises further above | drops far below
questions.rationale: A rise above the set point triggers faster breathing, which removes CO2 and returns it toward the set point, opposing the disturbance. Choosing 'decrease' or 'rises further above' would let CO2 keep climbing instead of stabilizing.

questions.stem: Choose the word that makes each statement about the feedback loop correct.
items: The rise in blood CO2 above the set point is the [ stimulus / response ] that the body detects.
Speeding up the breathing rate is the body's [ response / disturbance ].
Because breathing speeds up to lower CO2, this feedback [ opposes / adds to ] the original change.
questions.rationale: The detected rise in CO2 is the stimulus, faster breathing is the response, and because the response counters the rise it opposes the change, keeping the system stable. Labeling the response as the disturbance or saying it 'adds to' the change would describe a runaway loop.

questions.stem: Decide whether each statement about the investigation and its data is True or False.
rows: Because blood CO2 returned to the set point, the data are evidence that a feedback mechanism kept it stable.
Measuring blood CO2 at only one moment would be enough to show the feedback loop worked.
Recording both blood CO2 and breathing rate over time shows how the response is linked to the disturbance.
The return of blood CO2 to its starting level is evidence that the internal environment was kept stable.
questions.rationale: Evidence for homeostasis needs the measured return to the set point and both variables over time to link disturbance and response. A single reading cannot show a return, so that statement is false.

standards.pe_text: Use a model to illustrate the role of cellular division (mitosis) and differentiation in producing and maintaining complex organisms.

stimuli.title: Rebuilding A Lost Leg
stimuli.phenomenon: A salamander loses part of one of its legs to a predator. Instead of forming only scar tissue, the salamander slowly rebuilds the entire missing section. Over several weeks, cells near the wound begin dividing again and again, forming a small mound of new cells. These new cells then develop into the different kinds of cells the leg needs, including skin cells, muscle cells, and bone cells, until a working leg has regrown. Scientists sequenced the DNA of the regrown cells and compared it. They found that the skin, muscle, and bone cells all contain exactly the same chromosomes and the same complete set of genes, even though the cells look and act very differently. The table summarizes what the scientists found. In the questions that follow, you will use a model of cell division and differentiation to explain how one kind of parent cell can rebuild a limb made of many specialized cell types.

figure.caption: Table 1. Genetic material and active genes in three cell types from the regrown limb.

questions.stem: The table compares three cell types from the regrown limb. What do the data show about their genetic material?
options: Each cell type has a different number of chromosomes.
All three cell types contain the same chromosomes and the same complete genome.
The muscle cells are missing some chromosomes found in the skin cells.
Only the skin cells contain a full set of genes.
questions.rationale: Every row shows the same chromosome number (28) and a complete genome, so all three cell types carry identical genetic material; they differ only in which genes are switched on. A 'missing chromosomes' option reflects the misconception that specialized cells lose DNA.

questions.stem: Complete the explanation using the data. Genetic testing shows the skin, muscle, and bone cells in the regrown limb all contain [Drop-down 1] DNA. They look and work differently because [Drop-down 2].
dd: different genes are switched on in each cell type | each cell type carries a different set of genes | each cell has a different number of chromosomes
correct: different genes are switched on in each cell type
questions.rationale: Different cell types arise from differential gene expression, not from different genetic material. The distractors restate the common error that specialization comes from cells having different DNA.

questions.stem: Arrange the steps that rebuild the limb in the correct order.
items: Different cells switch on different genes and become skin, muscle, and bone cells.
Cells near the wound copy all of their DNA.
Each cell divides, forming daughter cells with the same complete set of genes.
Cell division repeats many times, producing a large number of new cells.
questions.rationale: DNA is copied before division, division yields genetically identical daughter cells, repeated division builds the cell mass, and differentiation comes last. Placing differentiation before division ignores that specialized cells arise from identical daughter cells.

questions.stem: Match each specialized cell type in the regrown limb to its main function.
questions.optset: cover and protect the new limb / contract to move the limb / provide rigid structural support
correct: cover and protect the new limb
questions.rationale: Differentiated cells form tissues with distinct structures and functions that together make a working limb. Mismatches show a gap in linking a cell's expressed identity to the function it carries out.

stimuli.title: Rebuilding Skin After A Cut
stimuli.phenomenon: When a person gets a shallow cut, the skin repairs itself over the following days. Skin cells near the edges of the wound begin to divide. Before each division, a cell copies all of its DNA, then splits into two daughter cells that each carry the same complete set of genes. These daughter cells divide again and again, filling in the gap. As the new cells build up, they differentiate: some switch on the genes that make them flat, protective surface cells, while others become the cells that form new blood vessels and connective tissue underneath. Genetic testing shows that all of these cells carry the same genome as the original skin cells; they differ only in which genes are switched on. The graph shows how the number of cells in the wound area changed during healing. In the questions that follow, you will use a model of cell division and differentiation to explain how the skin rebuilds itself.

figure.caption: Figure 1. The number of cells in the wound area over 8 days of healing.
figure.title: Cells in the Wound Area During Healing

questions.stem: According to the graph, what happened to the number of cells in the wound area over the 8 days?
options: It increased greatly as the cells divided again and again.
It stayed the same the whole time.
It decreased as cells were lost.
It fell to zero by day 8.
questions.rationale: The line climbs from 10 cells on day 0 to 300 by day 8 as repeated cell division fills the wound. The other options contradict the steady rise shown by the curve.

questions.stem: Choose the word or phrase that makes each statement correct.
items: As a skin cell divides, it first [ copies / discards ] all of its DNA.
Each daughter cell receives [ the same / a smaller ] complete set of genes as the parent cell.
The surface cells and blood-vessel cells look different because different [ genes / numbers of chromosomes ] are switched on.
questions.rationale: DNA is copied before division so each daughter cell gets the same complete set of genes, and cell types differ only in which genes are active. Choosing 'discards' or 'a smaller' set repeats the misconception that specialized cells lose genetic material.

questions.stem: Select all that apply. Which statements about the healed skin are supported by the information?
options: The different cell types all contain the same genome.
The cell types differ because different genes are switched on.
The surface skin cells lost some of their genes in order to specialize.
The new cells were produced by cell division.
Each daughter cell has a different number of chromosomes than the parent cell.
questions.rationale: The cells share one genome, differ by which genes are active, and arise from division. The unselected options state that specializing cells lose genes or change chromosome number, which the same-genome evidence contradicts.

questions.stem: Decide whether each statement about the healed skin is True or False.
rows: Cell division increased the number of cells, letting the wound fill in.
The specialized cells form tissues that carry out specific jobs, such as protecting the body.
The surface skin cells and the blood-vessel cells contain different genomes.
Differentiation lets identical daughter cells take on different jobs in the skin.
questions.rationale: Division supplies the new cells, and differentiation lets identical cells form tissues with distinct functions. The claim that the cell types have different genomes is false, because the testing showed one shared genome.

stimuli.title: From One Cell To Many
stimuli.phenomenon: Every person begins as a single cell. When a sperm cell and an egg cell join, they form one fertilized egg that holds a complete genome. This single cell divides into two cells, then four, then eight, and so on. Each division copies the whole genome, so every new cell carries the same complete set of genes. As the growing ball of cells gets larger, the cells begin to differentiate: some switch on the genes that make them muscle cells, while others become nerve cells, skin cells, or blood cells. In this way one fertilized egg gives rise to the many specialized cell types of the whole body, even though every cell contains the same genome. The table compares three cell types from a developing embryo. In the questions that follow, you will use a model of cell division and differentiation to explain how one cell can produce the many cell types of a complex organism.

figure.caption: Table 1. Three cell types from a developing embryo.

questions.stem: According to the table, how do the muscle, nerve, and skin cells compare?
options: They contain the same genome and the same number of chromosomes, but different genes are switched on.
They each contain a different genome.
They have different numbers of chromosomes.
Only the muscle cell contains a complete genome.
questions.rationale: Every row shows a complete genome and 46 chromosomes, and the cells differ only in the 'Genes switched on' column. The distractors claim differences in genome or chromosome number that the table does not show.

questions.stem: Arrange the steps in order (1 = first) to model how one fertilized egg produces many cell types.
items: The cell divides again and again, and every new cell keeps the full genome.
A sperm cell and an egg cell join to form a single fertilized egg.
Cells switch on different genes and become muscle, nerve, and skin cells.
The fertilized egg copies its whole genome and divides into two cells.
questions.rationale: Fertilization forms the first cell, which copies its genome and divides, divides repeatedly, and only then differentiates. Placing differentiation before the divisions ignores that the specialized cells come from identical daughter cells.

questions.stem: Complete the explanation using the data. The muscle cell and the nerve cell contain [Drop-down 1] genome. They develop into different types of cells because [Drop-down 2] in each cell, not because they contain [Drop-down 3] genetic material.
dd: different genes are switched on | different genes are deleted | extra chromosomes are added
questions.rationale: The cells share one genome and become different types through differential gene expression, not by carrying different DNA. The distractors restate the error that specialization comes from deleting genes or from different genetic material.

questions.stem: Decide whether each statement about the developing body is True or False.
rows: All of the specialized cells came from one fertilized egg through cell division.
Muscle cells and nerve cells contain different genomes.
The specialized cells form tissues and organs that carry out specific functions.
The differences among the cell types come from which genes are active, not from different DNA.
questions.rationale: One fertilized egg divides to produce all the cells, which form tissues and organs and differ only in active genes. The claim that muscle and nerve cells have different genomes is false, because the table shows the same genome in every cell.

standards.pe_text: Use a model to illustrate how photosynthesis transforms light energy into stored chemical energy.

stimuli.title: Bubbles In The Light
stimuli.phenomenon: A student places a sprig of a green water plant in a beaker of water and shines a lamp on it. Tiny bubbles of gas rise from the cut end of the stem. The student counts the bubbles released each minute as a measure of how fast the plant is making food. Then the lamp is moved to different distances, changing how much light reaches the plant, and the counting is repeated at each light level. At very low light, few bubbles form. As the light gets brighter, the plant releases bubbles faster, until the rate finally levels off and stops increasing. The plant is using energy from light to build sugar molecules inside its chloroplasts, and oxygen is given off in the process. The graph shows how the rate changed with light intensity. In the questions that follow, you will use a model of photosynthesis to describe how light energy is transformed into chemical energy stored in sugar.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Rate of oxygen release by a water plant at increasing light intensities.
figure.title: Rate of Photosynthesis vs. Light Intensity

questions.stem: The graph shows how the rate of photosynthesis in the water plant changes with light intensity. Which statement best describes the pattern?
options: As light intensity increases, the rate of photosynthesis decreases steadily.
As light intensity increases, the rate of photosynthesis increases and then levels off.
The rate of photosynthesis does not change as light intensity increases.
The rate of photosynthesis is highest at the lowest light intensity.
questions.rationale: More light energy speeds photosynthesis until another factor limits it, so the curve rises then plateaus. Reading it as flat or decreasing misses the connection between the energy input and the rate of the product's release.

questions.stem: Complete the model of matter and energy in photosynthesis. In photosynthesis, a plant takes in [Drop-down 1] and water from its surroundings. Using energy captured from [Drop-down 2], the chloroplasts produce [Drop-down 3], which store the energy in their chemical bonds.
dd: sunlight | heat in the soil | oxygen
sugar molecules | water molecules | mineral crystals
questions.rationale: Carbon dioxide and water are the matter inputs, light is the energy input, and sugar is the product that stores chemical energy. The distractors swap inputs for outputs or treat oxygen as an energy source.

questions.stem: Select all that apply. Which substances are products (outputs) of photosynthesis?
options: Sugar
Oxygen
Carbon dioxide
Water
Sunlight
questions.rationale: Sugar and oxygen are produced; carbon dioxide and water are reactants, and sunlight is an energy input rather than a material product. Selecting a reactant shows the outputs and inputs of matter have been confused.

questions.stem: Choose the word that makes each statement about energy and matter correct.
items: Photosynthesis [ stores / releases ] energy in chemical bonds.
The energy that drives photosynthesis comes from [ light / heat ].
That captured energy is stored in the bonds of [ sugar / oxygen ] molecules.
questions.rationale: Photosynthesis transforms light energy into chemical energy stored in the bonds of sugar. Choosing 'releases' or 'oxygen' confuses this energy-storing process with a process that transfers energy out of chemical bonds.

stimuli.title: Turning Up The Carbon Dioxide
stimuli.phenomenon: A researcher grows tomato seedlings in a sealed clear chamber kept under bright, constant light and a comfortable temperature. She changes only one thing: the amount of carbon dioxide in the air around the leaves. At each setting she measures how fast the plant makes sugar by tracking how quickly the leaves take in carbon dioxide. When the air holds very little carbon dioxide, the plant makes sugar slowly. As she raises the carbon dioxide concentration, the plant makes sugar faster and faster. Beyond a certain point, adding still more carbon dioxide no longer speeds things up, and the rate levels off. The plant is capturing energy from light and using the carbon and oxygen atoms from carbon dioxide, along with water, to build sugar inside its chloroplasts. The graph shows how the rate of sugar production changed with carbon dioxide concentration. In the questions that follow, you will use a model of photosynthesis to explain how matter and energy move as light energy is stored in sugar.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Rate of sugar production by a plant at increasing carbon dioxide concentrations.
figure.title: Rate of Photosynthesis vs. Carbon Dioxide

questions.stem: The graph shows how the rate of sugar production changes with carbon dioxide concentration. Which statement best describes the pattern?
options: As carbon dioxide concentration increases, the rate of sugar production steadily decreases.
As carbon dioxide concentration increases, the rate of sugar production increases and then levels off.
The rate of sugar production stays the same at every carbon dioxide concentration.
The rate of sugar production is highest when carbon dioxide is lowest.
questions.rationale: More carbon dioxide supplies more carbon atoms for building sugar, so the rate climbs until another factor limits it and the curve plateaus. Reading the curve as flat or decreasing misses the link between the matter input and the amount of product made.

questions.stem: A student builds a model to show how the plant stores light energy in sugar. Put the steps in the correct order (1 = first).
items: Sugar molecules form, storing chemical energy in their bonds.
The leaf takes in carbon dioxide from the air and water from the soil.
Chlorophyll in the chloroplasts captures energy from light.
The captured energy is used to combine the atoms into new molecules.
questions.rationale: Photosynthesis begins by taking in the raw materials (matter) and capturing light (energy), then uses that energy to build sugar, which stores the energy in its bonds. Placing sugar formation before the materials are taken in reverses the flow of matter and energy.

questions.stem: Decide whether each statement about the plant's matter and energy is True or False.
rows: The carbon atoms in the plant's new sugar come from carbon dioxide in the air.
Light energy is transformed into chemical energy stored in the sugar.
The plant creates new atoms in order to build the sugar molecules.
Raising the carbon dioxide supply provided more matter for building sugar.
questions.rationale: Photosynthesis rearranges existing atoms (carbon from carbon dioxide, hydrogen and oxygen from water) and transforms light energy into chemical energy in sugar; it never creates atoms. Recognizing the false statement shows that matter is conserved.

questions.stem: Select all that apply. Starting from the point where the rate has leveled off, which changes would slow the plant's production of sugar?
options: Turning off the light
Removing the carbon dioxide from the air
Cutting off the plant's water supply
Adding even more carbon dioxide
Keeping the light and carbon dioxide exactly the same
questions.rationale: Sugar production needs both an energy input (light) and matter inputs (carbon dioxide and water), so removing any one slows or stops it. Adding more carbon dioxide past the plateau or changing nothing would not slow the rate.

stimuli.title: Light, Dark, And Stored Starch
stimuli.phenomenon: Green plants make sugar in the light and store any extra as starch, a compact way to keep chemical energy. A gardener tests this. First she keeps a leafy plant in complete darkness for two days so its leaves use up the starch already stored. Then she covers part of one leaf with foil so no light can reach it and places the plant in bright light for a day. She also keeps a second plant in the dark the whole time. Afterward she uses iodine, which stains starch blue-black, to measure how much starch each leaf holds. The parts of leaves that received light are full of starch, the foil-covered part has almost none, and the plant left in the dark has none at all. The graph shows the relative amount of starch found in each case. In the questions that follow, you will use these results as evidence that light energy is stored as chemical energy in the sugar and starch a plant makes.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Relative amount of starch found in leaf tissue after different light exposure.
figure.title: Starch Stored After Different Light Exposure

questions.stem: According to the graph, which leaf tissue stored the most starch?
options: The leaf tissue that received light
The leaf area covered by foil
The plant kept in the dark
All three stored the same amount of starch
questions.rationale: Starch, a store of chemical energy, built up only where light reached the leaf. The covered area and the dark-kept plant made almost none, showing that light is required to store the energy.

questions.stem: Match each part of the investigation to its role in the plant's storage of energy.
questions.optset: energy source captured by the plant / raw materials that supply the atoms / place where sugar is made / where the chemical energy is stored
correct: energy source captured by the plant
raw materials that supply the atoms
where the chemical energy is stored
questions.rationale: Light is the energy input, carbon dioxide and water supply the matter, the chloroplast is where sugar is built, and starch is the store of chemical energy. Matching them shows how energy and matter move through the model.

questions.stem: Decide whether each statement is True or False.
rows: The starch in the lighted leaf stores chemical energy that came from light.
The plant kept in the dark could still store starch without light.
Making and storing starch is a way the plant saves captured energy for later.
The energy in the starch was created by the plant from nothing.
questions.rationale: The results show starch forms only with light, so its stored chemical energy is transformed from light energy rather than created from nothing, and a plant in the dark cannot make it.

questions.stem: Complete each prediction using the results. If the gardener had left the foil on the whole leaf, that leaf would have stored [Drop-down 1] starch, because it was missing the [Drop-down 2] it needs to make sugar. This shows that a plant stores chemical energy only when it can capture [Drop-down 3].
dd: light | heat from the air | oxygen
questions.rationale: Without light a leaf cannot carry out photosynthesis, so it stores no new starch. The prediction follows the pattern in the data that light energy is required to build and store sugar.

standards.pe_text: Construct and revise an explanation based on evidence for how carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen from sugar molecules may combine with other elements to form amino acids and/or other large carbon-based molecules.

stimuli.title: Building Bigger Molecules
stimuli.phenomenon: As a plant grows, it does not take in large molecules ready-made — it builds them. During the day the plant makes many small sugar molecules, each made of only carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atoms. To grow new stems, leaves, and roots, the plant's cells link large numbers of these sugar molecules together into much larger carbon-based molecules. For example, cellulose — the tough material that forms plant cell walls and wood — is a long chain built from many sugar units. To build proteins, the plant rearranges atoms from sugar and adds nitrogen atoms taken up from the soil. In every case the atoms in the large molecules come from smaller molecules the plant already had: no atoms are created or destroyed, they are only rearranged and combined. The table compares three molecules in the plant. In the questions that follow, you will use this information to explain how atoms from sugar combine with other elements to form larger carbon-based molecules.

figure.caption: Table 1. Three molecules a plant uses, the elements they contain, and their relative size.
rows: Large — a chain of many sugars

questions.stem: According to the table, which element is found in the plant's protein but not in its sugar or cellulose?
options: Carbon
Hydrogen
Oxygen
Nitrogen
questions.rationale: Protein's row lists nitrogen in addition to C, H, O; to build protein the plant adds nitrogen to atoms taken from sugar.

questions.stem: Select all statements about building larger molecules that are supported by the information.
options: Cellulose is built by linking together many small sugar molecules.
The carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atoms in cellulose come from sugar molecules.
New atoms are created when the plant builds a larger molecule.
Building a protein requires an element that sugar does not contain.
A single sugar molecule is larger than a cellulose molecule.
questions.rationale: A, B, D follow from the table and conservation of matter; C (atoms created) and E (sugar larger than cellulose) are the misconceptions.

questions.stem: Complete the explanation. To build a large molecule such as cellulose, the plant [Drop-down 1] many sugar molecules. The atoms are not created — they are [Drop-down 2] from the smaller molecules. To build a protein instead of cellulose, the plant must also add [Drop-down 3].
questions.rationale: Larger molecules are assembled by linking sugars and rearranging their atoms (matter conserved); protein additionally needs nitrogen.

questions.stem: Decide whether each statement is True or False.
rows: The mass of the plant's new cellulose comes from the atoms in the sugar molecules it already made.
When the plant builds larger molecules, some atoms are created out of nothing.
A plant with no source of nitrogen would have trouble building proteins.
questions.rationale: Matter is conserved — the mass comes from existing atoms, none created; nitrogen is required for protein, so its absence limits protein building.

stimuli.title: Building A Caterpillar's Body
stimuli.phenomenon: A newly hatched caterpillar is smaller than a grain of rice. Over about two weeks it does almost nothing but eat leaves, and it grows so fast that its mass increases hundreds of times before it forms a chrysalis. The leaves it eats are rich in sugar, which is made of only carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atoms, and they also supply small amounts of nitrogen. As the caterpillar grows, it builds new body tissues, including stored fat and body protein. To make fat, its cells rearrange and link atoms from sugar. To make protein, its cells combine atoms from sugar with nitrogen. In every case the atoms in the caterpillar's growing body come from the food it has eaten; no atoms are created or destroyed. The graph shows how one caterpillar's mass changed as it fed. In the questions that follow, you will explain how atoms from food sugar combine with other elements to build the larger molecules of a growing body.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Mass of one caterpillar measured over 16 days of feeding.
figure.title: Caterpillar Mass During Growth

questions.stem: The graph shows the caterpillar's mass over 16 days. Which statement is best supported by the data?
options: The caterpillar's mass increased many times over as it ate and grew.
The caterpillar's mass stayed about the same over the 16 days.
The caterpillar lost mass as it grew older.
The caterpillar's mass came from the air, not from its food.
questions.rationale: The bars climb from a few milligrams to several thousand, showing a large mass increase. Because a caterpillar builds its body from the food it eats, this increase is evidence that it is constructing new body molecules from its leaf food.

questions.stem: Put the steps in order (1 = first) to show how atoms from leaf food become part of the caterpillar's body.
items: The small molecules are rearranged and linked into larger fat and protein molecules.
The caterpillar eats leaves that contain sugar and other small molecules.
The caterpillar's body mass increases as the new molecules build its tissues.
The food is broken down into small molecules inside the caterpillar.
questions.rationale: Matter flows from ingested food to body tissue: the caterpillar takes in food, breaks it into small molecules, rearranges and links those atoms into larger molecules, and its body grows. The atoms are conserved throughout.

questions.stem: Match each body molecule to what the caterpillar needs to build it.
questions.right: What is needed to build it
questions.optset: built from sugar's atoms only / also needs nitrogen added
questions.rationale: Fat is built from the carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen already present in sugar, while protein additionally requires nitrogen. Distinguishing them shows that building some molecules means combining sugar's atoms with another element.

questions.stem: Select all that apply. A caterpillar is fed a food that contains sugar but almost no nitrogen. Based on the model, which predictions are correct?
options: It could still build stored fat, which needs only carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen.
It would have trouble building body protein, which also needs nitrogen.
It could create nitrogen atoms from the sugar to make protein.
The atoms in any new fat would come from the sugar it ate.
It could build protein just as easily without any nitrogen.
questions.rationale: Fat needs only the carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen supplied by sugar, so it can still be built, but protein additionally requires nitrogen, which cannot be created from sugar. The false options ignore conservation of matter.

stimuli.title: Sugar Into Stored Seed Oil
stimuli.phenomenon: On a sunflower head, hundreds of seeds ripen over several weeks. The parent plant makes sugar in its leaves and sends it to each developing seed. Inside the seed, this sugar is not simply stored as sugar. Instead, the seed's cells rearrange the carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atoms from many sugar molecules and link them into oil, a compact, energy-rich material that will later help a new seedling grow. Scientists sampled seeds at different times during ripening and measured the sugar and oil they contained, as a percent of the seed's dry mass. Over the weeks, the amount of sugar in the seeds steadily fell while the amount of oil steadily rose. No atoms were created or destroyed; the atoms that had been in the sugar ended up in the larger oil molecules. The graph shows how the sugar and oil content changed as the seeds ripened. In the questions that follow, you will use this evidence to explain how atoms from sugar are built into larger carbon-based molecules.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Sugar and oil content of sunflower seeds during ripening.
figure.title: Sugar and Oil in Ripening Seeds

questions.stem: Which pattern in the graph is the best evidence that the seed builds oil using atoms from sugar?
options: As the seeds ripen, the sugar content falls while the oil content rises.
As the seeds ripen, both sugar and oil content rise together.
As the seeds ripen, both sugar and oil content fall together.
The sugar and oil content stay the same during ripening.
questions.rationale: The sugar decreases over the same period that the oil increases, which fits the idea that atoms once in sugar are being rearranged and built into oil. The other options do not match the opposing trends in the data.

questions.stem: Complete the description of what happens inside the seed. The seed receives [Drop-down 1] from the parent plant. Its cells link the carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atoms into larger [Drop-down 2] molecules. The atoms are not created; they are only [Drop-down 3].
questions.rationale: Matter flows from sugar into oil as the seed rearranges the same atoms into larger molecules. Because atoms are conserved, they are rearranged rather than created or destroyed.

questions.stem: Decide whether each statement is True or False.
rows: The carbon atoms in the seed's oil came from the sugar the seed received.
Oil molecules are larger than the sugar molecules used to build them.
The seed created new atoms in order to make the oil.
Sugar and oil are both built only from carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen.
questions.rationale: Oil is a larger molecule assembled from the carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atoms of sugar, with no atoms created. Recognizing the false statement shows that matter is conserved as smaller molecules are built into larger ones.

questions.stem: Choose the word or phrase that makes each prediction correct.
items: If the parent plant sent the seed more sugar, the seed could build [ more / less ] oil.
The extra mass stored as oil comes from [ the sugar / the sunlight ] delivered to the seed.
To build oil instead of protein, the seed does [ not need / need ] to add nitrogen.
questions.rationale: More sugar supplies more atoms to build oil, and that stored mass comes from the sugar's atoms. Because oil contains only carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen, no nitrogen is required, unlike protein.

standards.pe_text: Use a model to illustrate that cellular respiration is a chemical process whereby the bonds of food molecules and oxygen molecules are broken and the bonds in new compounds are formed, resulting in a net transfer of energy.

stimuli.title: Seeds That Breathe
stimuli.phenomenon: In a biology investigation, students measure how much oxygen different samples use. They place germinating (sprouting) pea seeds in one sealed tube, an equal volume of dry pea seeds in a second tube, and an equal volume of glass beads in a third tube. Each tube is connected to a thin measuring tube so that any oxygen used by the sample can be tracked. After one hour at room temperature, the students find that the germinating seeds have used a large amount of oxygen, the dry seeds have used only a little, and the glass beads have used none at all. The germinating seeds are alive and actively growing, breaking down their stored food to release the energy they need. The graph shows the oxygen used by each sample. In the questions that follow, you will use a model of cellular respiration to explain how food and oxygen are transformed into new compounds and usable energy.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Oxygen used per hour by three samples in sealed tubes.
figure.title: Oxygen Used by Different Samples

questions.stem: The graph shows the oxygen used by each sample. Which sample used the most oxygen, and why?
options: The glass beads, because they are the densest sample.
The dry peas, because they hold the most stored food.
The germinating peas, because their living, growing cells carry out cellular respiration.
All three used the same amount because oxygen spreads out evenly.
questions.rationale: Only the actively growing seeds run cellular respiration fast enough to consume noticeable oxygen; the beads are nonliving and the dry seeds are barely active. The distractors attribute oxygen use to density or storage rather than to a living process.

questions.stem: Match each substance to its role in cellular respiration.
questions.optset: reactant (input) / product (output)
questions.rationale: Food and oxygen are the reactants whose bonds are broken; carbon dioxide and water are the products whose bonds are formed. Reversing any role shows a mix-up of the inputs and outputs of the process.

questions.stem: Select all that apply. Which statements correctly describe matter and energy during cellular respiration?
options: The atoms in the carbon dioxide and water released came from the food and oxygen.
Energy is transferred, not created, when bonds are broken and new bonds form.
New atoms are created as the food is broken down.
The total number of atoms stays the same before and after the process.
Matter is destroyed when energy is released.
questions.rationale: Cellular respiration rearranges existing atoms and transfers stored energy; it does not create or destroy matter. The unselected options express the misconception that atoms or matter can appear or vanish.

questions.stem: Choose the word or phrase that makes each statement about cellular respiration correct.
items: During cellular respiration, the cell breaks the bonds in food and [ oxygen / nitrogen ].
New bonds form in the products, which are [ carbon dioxide and water / sugar and oxygen ].
The energy released is captured by the cell in molecules of [ ATP / DNA ].
questions.rationale: Food plus oxygen react to form carbon dioxide and water, and the released energy is stored in ATP. Choosing sugar and oxygen as products or DNA as the energy carrier reverses the reaction or confuses energy storage with genetic material.

stimuli.title: Oxygen Use During Exercise
stimuli.phenomenon: A person rides a stationary exercise bike while a machine measures the gases she breathes. It records how much oxygen her body takes in and how much carbon dioxide she breathes out each minute. While she sits at rest, both numbers are low. As the bike is set to light, then moderate, then hard effort, her working leg muscles need more and more energy. To release that energy, the muscles break down food molecules using oxygen, and they give off carbon dioxide and water in the process. The machine shows that as her effort increases, both the oxygen she uses and the carbon dioxide she produces climb together. The graph shows the two measurements at each level of effort. In the questions that follow, you will use a model of cellular respiration to explain how food and oxygen are transformed into usable energy and new compounds, and how matter and energy are conserved.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Oxygen used and carbon dioxide produced at increasing levels of effort.
figure.title: Gas Exchange During Exercise

questions.stem: The graph shows the oxygen used and carbon dioxide produced at each level of effort. Which statement best describes the relationship?
options: As effort increases, oxygen use rises but carbon dioxide production falls.
As effort increases, both oxygen use and carbon dioxide production rise together.
As effort increases, both oxygen use and carbon dioxide production fall.
Oxygen use and carbon dioxide production are not related to effort.
questions.rationale: Oxygen is a reactant taken in and carbon dioxide is a product given off, so as the muscles carry out more cellular respiration both rise together. Reading them as opposite or unrelated misses the reactant-to-product link.

questions.stem: Complete the explanation of what the muscles are doing. The rising oxygen use shows the muscles are taking in more [Drop-down 1] to break down [Drop-down 2]. This releases energy the muscles can use and gives off [Drop-down 3] as a product.
questions.rationale: Cellular respiration uses oxygen and food as reactants and releases energy plus carbon dioxide and water. The distractors swap a reactant for a product or name substances not involved.

questions.stem: Decide whether each statement about matter and energy is True or False.
rows: The carbon atoms in the carbon dioxide she breathes out came from the food she ate.
The energy released by her muscles was already stored in the food molecules.
Her muscles create new energy that did not exist before.
Atoms are destroyed when the food molecules are broken down.
questions.rationale: Cellular respiration rearranges existing atoms and transfers energy that was already stored in food; energy and matter are conserved, not created or destroyed, so the last two statements are false.

questions.stem: Put the steps of cellular respiration in order (1 = first) to show how the muscles get usable energy.
items: The atoms are rearranged, forming new carbon dioxide and water molecules.
Food molecules and oxygen are taken in by the muscle cells.
Energy is released for the muscle to use, and carbon dioxide is breathed out.
The bonds in the food and oxygen molecules are broken apart.
questions.rationale: The model runs from reactants to products: food and oxygen are taken in, their bonds are broken, the atoms are rearranged into carbon dioxide and water, and the stored energy is released for the muscle. Reversing the order would put products before reactants.

stimuli.title: Yeast With And Without Oxygen
stimuli.phenomenon: Baker's yeast are tiny living organisms that get energy by breaking down sugar. A student sets up two flasks that each contain the same amount of yeast and the same amount of sugar water. Flask A is left open to the air, so the yeast have plenty of oxygen. Flask B is sealed tight, so once the yeast use up the small amount of oxygen inside, they must break down sugar without it. The student measures how much usable energy the yeast release from each gram of sugar and whether carbon dioxide gas is given off. In Flask A, with oxygen, the yeast release a large amount of energy from each gram of sugar. In Flask B, without oxygen, the yeast still break down sugar and still give off carbon dioxide, but they release far less energy from each gram. The table shows the results. In the questions that follow, you will use a model of cellular respiration to explain how breaking down food releases energy and how matter and energy are conserved.

figure.caption: Table 1. Energy released and gas given off by yeast breaking down sugar, with and without oxygen.
columns: Energy released per gram of sugar (relative units)

questions.stem: According to the table, how does the presence of oxygen affect the energy the yeast release from each gram of sugar?
options: With oxygen, the yeast release much more energy from each gram of sugar.
With oxygen, the yeast release much less energy from each gram of sugar.
Oxygen makes no difference to the energy released.
Without oxygen, the yeast cannot break down sugar at all.
questions.rationale: Flask A (with oxygen) shows 100 units of energy per gram versus only 7 in Flask B (without oxygen), so oxygen greatly increases the energy released. The last option is wrong because Flask B still breaks down sugar and releases carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: Select all that apply. Which statements about matter and energy are correct for the yeast in both flasks?
options: The energy the yeast release was already stored in the bonds of the sugar.
The carbon in the carbon dioxide given off came from the sugar.
The yeast create new energy that was not present before.
The atoms in the sugar are rearranged into new products, not destroyed.
Matter disappears when the yeast release energy.
questions.rationale: Breaking down sugar transfers energy that was already stored and rearranges the sugar's atoms into products such as carbon dioxide; energy and matter are conserved, so nothing is created or destroyed.

questions.stem: Complete each statement using the results. Sealing the flask removes the yeast's supply of [Drop-down 1]. Without it, the yeast release [Drop-down 2] energy from each gram of sugar, but they still give off [Drop-down 3].
questions.rationale: Removing oxygen (the sealed flask) lowers the energy released from each gram of sugar, as the data show, but the yeast still break down sugar and release carbon dioxide. This predicts the effect of removing a reactant.

questions.stem: Choose the word or phrase that makes each statement correct.
items: For the yeast, sugar is a [ reactant / product ] that is broken down.
The energy the yeast use is stored in the [ bonds / color ] of the sugar.
The yeast release more usable energy from each gram of sugar when [ oxygen is present / oxygen is absent ].
questions.rationale: Sugar is a reactant whose chemical bonds hold the stored energy, and the yeast release much more of that energy when oxygen is available, as the data show.

standards.pe_text: Use mathematical and/or computational representations to support explanations of factors that affect carrying capacity of ecosystems at different scales.

stimuli.title: Reindeer On St. Matthew Island
stimuli.phenomenon: In 1944, 29 reindeer were released onto St. Matthew Island, a remote, treeless island in the Bering Sea. The island had no wolves or other predators, and it was covered with a thick mat of slow-growing lichen that reindeer feed on during the long winter. With plenty of food and no predators, the herd grew quickly. By 1957 biologists counted about 1,350 reindeer, and by the summer of 1963 the herd had exploded to roughly 6,000 animals. That winter, however, the reindeer had eaten almost all of the lichen faster than it could regrow. During the harsh winter of 1963-1964, thousands of reindeer starved. By 1966 only 42 reindeer were left alive on the island. The graph shows how the population changed over these years. In the questions that follow, you will use the data to explain how a limiting resource affected the carrying capacity of the island.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Reindeer population on St. Matthew Island, 1944-1966.
figure.title: Reindeer Population on St. Matthew Island
figure.source: Data: Klein, 1968, Journal of Wildlife Management.

questions.stem: According to the graph, in which year was the reindeer population the largest?
questions.rationale: The line peaks at about 6,000 reindeer in 1963. Choosing 1966 confuses the crash (42 animals) with the peak; choosing 1957 stops at an intermediate value of about 1,350.

questions.stem: From 1963 to 1966, the population fell by about [Drop-down 1] reindeer. Such a large drop shows that the herd had grown far above the island's [Drop-down 2].
questions.rationale: 6,000 - 42 is about 5,958, which rounds to roughly 6,000. Because the lichen (the limiting resource) could not support so many animals, the herd exceeded the island's carrying capacity and crashed. '3,000' halves the change, and '1,300' confuses the 1957 count with the loss.

questions.stem: Order the events on St. Matthew Island from first to last to show how the reindeer population rose and then crashed.
items: Reindeer overgraze and nearly eliminate the island's lichen
29 reindeer are released onto an island that has no predators
The herd grows to about 6,000 animals
Thousands of reindeer starve and the population crashes to 42
questions.rationale: The correct order is release, rapid growth, overgrazing of the limiting resource, then the crash. The population overshot the carrying capacity before the food ran out, so overgrazing comes after the herd is already large.

questions.stem: Select all of the factors that would lower the carrying capacity of St. Matthew Island for reindeer.
options: Loss of lichen from overgrazing
A colder winter that kills more of the lichen
A plant disease that kills much of the lichen
An increase in the amount of lichen on the island
A larger island with the same total amount of food
questions.rationale: Carrying capacity is set by the limiting resource (lichen) and conditions: losing lichen to overgrazing, a colder winter that kills lichen, and a disease that kills lichen all shrink the food supply and lower carrying capacity. More lichen or a larger island would raise it.

stimuli.title: Hare And Lynx Cycles
stimuli.phenomenon: Snowshoe hares and Canada lynx live in the northern forests of Canada. For almost 200 years, fur trappers sold their pelts to the Hudson's Bay Company, which kept careful records of how many of each animal were traded every year. These long records reveal a striking pattern: the numbers of hares and lynx rise and fall together in a repeating cycle of about ten years. Snowshoe hares are plant-eaters, and lynx are predators that feed almost entirely on hares. When hares are plentiful, the lynx have abundant food and their numbers climb. As predators become abundant, so many hares are caught that the hare population crashes, and soon afterward the starving lynx population falls too. Then the hares recover and the cycle begins again. The table shows counts, in thousands of animals, from one stretch of these records. In the questions that follow, you will use the data to explain how predation and food supply act as limiting factors that keep each population near a fluctuating balance.

figure.caption: Table 1. Snowshoe hare and lynx numbers from fur-trade records (thousands of animals).
figure.source: Data: based on Hudson's Bay Company fur-trade records (MacLulich, 1937).

questions.stem: According to the table, in which year was the snowshoe hare population the largest?
options: 1905 (40 thousand)
1907 (130 thousand)
1911 (12 thousand)
1914 (120 thousand)
questions.rationale: The hare count peaks at 130 thousand in 1907. Choosing 1914 (120 thousand) grabs a high value that is still slightly lower than the 1907 peak; 1911 is the low point, not the high.

questions.stem: From its peak in 1907 to its low in 1911, the snowshoe hare count fell by about [Drop-down 1] thousand. Over that same time, the lynx population [Drop-down 2], because its main source of food had become scarce.
dd: also fell | rose sharply | stayed the same
