questions.rationale: 130 thousand minus 12 thousand is about 118 thousand. As the hares (the lynx's food) crashed, the lynx fell from 30 thousand in 1907 to 8 thousand in 1911. Choosing 12 or 60 misreads or halves the change.

questions.stem: Decide whether each statement about the data is True or False.
rows: The lynx population reaches its peak in the same year as or just after the hare peak.
The lynx population is controlled mainly by the supply of snowshoe hares, its food.
The hare and lynx populations rise and fall independently of each other.
When the hare population crashed after 1907, the lynx population fell soon afterward.
questions.rationale: Hares peak in 1907 and lynx in 1908, and the lynx crash follows the hare crash, so the two are linked through predation, not independent. The false statement reveals the misconception that predator and prey change separately.

questions.stem: Choose the word or phrase that makes each statement correct.
items: When snowshoe hares become very abundant, the lynx population soon [ rises / falls ].
Heavy predation by lynx is a limiting factor that makes the hare population [ grow without limit / fall ].
Because each population responds to the other, their numbers [ fluctuate in a repeating cycle / stay constant ] over time.
questions.rationale: Abundant prey lets predators increase; heavy predation then drives prey down; the back-and-forth produces the repeating cycle. Picking 'grow without limit' or 'stay constant' ignores how predation and food supply limit each population.

stimuli.title: Yeast Reaching A Limit
stimuli.phenomenon: Yeast are tiny single-celled fungi used to make bread and other foods. A student adds a small amount of yeast to a flask filled with sugar-water and keeps it warm. Each day the student stirs the flask and counts the number of yeast cells, measured in millions of cells per milliliter. At first there are only a few yeast and plenty of sugar, so the population grows slowly. Then, as the yeast multiply, the population grows faster and faster. After several days the growth slows down, and the population finally levels off near 120 million cells per milliliter and stays there. By then the sugar, which is the yeast's limiting resource, is nearly used up, and wastes have built up in the water, so the flask can support only so many yeast. This leveling-off number is the carrying capacity of the flask. In the questions that follow, you will use the data to explain how a limiting resource sets the carrying capacity of this small ecosystem.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Yeast population in a flask of sugar-water over 10 days.
figure.title: Yeast Population in a Flask

questions.stem: According to the graph, what is the approximate carrying capacity of the flask for yeast?
options: About 2 million cells/mL
About 60 million cells/mL
About 120 million cells/mL
About 140 million cells/mL
questions.rationale: Carrying capacity is the level the curve flattens out at, about 120 million cells/mL. 2 is the starting value, 60 is a midpoint during rapid growth, and 140 is just the top of the axis.

questions.stem: Select all that apply. Which factors caused the yeast population to stop increasing after about day 7?
options: The sugar the yeast use for food was being used up.
Wastes built up in the flask.
The flask could support only a limited number of yeast.
The yeast ran out of predators to eat them.
The temperature in the flask dropped below freezing.
questions.rationale: Running low on the limiting resource (sugar) and the build-up of wastes set the flask's carrying capacity, so growth stops. Predators and freezing are not part of this scenario and are distractors.

questions.stem: Arrange the phases of the yeast population's growth in the order they occur, from first to last.
items: Growth slows as the sugar starts to run low.
The population levels off at the carrying capacity.
The population grows slowly at first, when there are only a few yeast.
The population grows quickly as the yeast multiply.
questions.rationale: The population starts slow, speeds up as numbers build, slows as the limiting resource runs low, and finally levels off at carrying capacity. Placing the leveling-off before the slowdown ignores that the resource must run low first.

questions.stem: Match each change to the way it would affect the flask's carrying capacity for yeast.
rows: Start the flask with more sugar
Start the flask with less sugar
Start with the same amount of sugar
questions.optset: raises the carrying capacity / lowers the carrying capacity / no change to the carrying capacity
correct: no change to the carrying capacity
questions.rationale: Because sugar is the limiting resource, more of it supports more yeast (higher carrying capacity) and less of it supports fewer. Keeping it the same leaves the carrying capacity unchanged.

standards.pe_text: Use mathematical representations to support and revise explanations, based on evidence about factors affecting biodiversity and populations in ecosystems of different scales.

stimuli.title: Birds In Broken Forests
stimuli.phenomenon: When a large forest is cleared for farms and roads, the trees that remain are left in separate patches, called fragments, of different sizes. Ecologists studied five forest fragments in a lowland region and counted the number of bird species living in each one. The smallest fragment, only 1 hectare in size, was home to just 8 bird species. A 25-hectare fragment held 24 species, and the largest fragment, 500 hectares, supported 41 species. The scientists noticed that larger fragments were home to a greater variety of birds, while the smallest patches had lost many species that need large areas of unbroken forest. This pattern, in which biodiversity falls as a habitat is broken into smaller pieces, is an example of habitat fragmentation. The table shows the area and the bird species richness of each fragment. In the questions that follow, you will use the data to explain how the size of a habitat is related to its biodiversity.

figure.caption: Table 1. Area and bird species richness of five forest fragments.

questions.stem: Using the table, about how many times as many bird species does the largest fragment (E, 500 ha) have as the smallest fragment (A, 1 ha)?
options: About the same number
About 2 times as many
About 5 times as many
About 40 times as many
questions.rationale: 41 species divided by 8 species is about 5; students compute from the table. (Note 500x the area holds only ~5x the species.)

questions.stem: As the area of a forest fragment increases, the number of bird species generally [Drop-down 1]. This means that breaking a large forest into small pieces tends to [Drop-down 2] biodiversity.
questions.rationale: The data rise from 8 species at 1 hectare to 41 species at 500 hectares, so species richness increases with area. Therefore habitat fragmentation, which leaves only small patches, lowers biodiversity.

questions.stem: Using the table, match each forest fragment to how its species richness compares with the others.
questions.optset: lowest / middle / highest
questions.rationale: Fragment A has 8 species (lowest), Fragment C has 24 species (middle of the three), and Fragment E has 41 species (highest). The ranking follows the increase in area.

questions.stem: A student claims, 'The data show that larger forest fragments support more bird species.' Decide whether each statement about this claim is True or False.
rows: The data support the student's claim.
Fragment E has both the largest area and the greatest species richness.
The 1-hectare fragment has more species than the 100-hectare fragment.
questions.rationale: Species richness rises steadily with area, so the claim is supported and Fragment E is both largest and richest. The last statement is false because the 1-hectare fragment has only 8 species while the 100-hectare fragment has 33.

stimuli.title: Islands And Their Species
stimuli.phenomenon: Islands are natural places to study biodiversity. Because an island is surrounded by water, the plants and animals living on it are separated from those on the mainland. Ecologists have long noticed that some islands are home to many more species than others. Two features seem to matter most: the size of the island and how far it lies from the mainland. Larger islands offer more space and more kinds of habitat, so they can support more species. Islands far from the mainland are harder for new species to reach, because few organisms can cross a wide stretch of ocean, so distant islands tend to have fewer species. Scientists surveyed five islands and counted the number of land bird species living on each, along with each island's area and its distance from the mainland. The table shows what they found. In the questions that follow, you will use the data to explain how island size and isolation affect the number of species an island can support.

figure.caption: Table 1. Area, distance from the mainland, and number of land bird species for five islands.

questions.stem: Islands P and Q both have an area of 10 km2. According to the table, which island has more bird species, and why?
options: Island P, because it lies closer to the mainland.
Island Q, because it lies farther from the mainland.
They have the same number, because they are the same size.
Island Q, because greater distance always means more species.
questions.rationale: With area held equal, Island P (20 km away, 12 species) beats Island Q (300 km away, 6 species), so being closer supports more species. The distractors reverse the isolation effect or ignore distance entirely.

questions.stem: Select all that apply. Which comparisons use two islands of different sizes but similar distances, so they show that larger islands hold more species?
options: Islands P and R (both near the mainland; 10 km2 vs 100 km2)
Islands R and T (both near the mainland; 100 km2 vs 1000 km2)
Islands Q and S (both far from the mainland; 10 km2 vs 100 km2)
Islands P and S (one near and one far; 10 km2 vs 100 km2)
Islands T and Q (one near and one far; 1000 km2 vs 10 km2)
questions.rationale: A fair test of area keeps distance about the same; P-R, R-T, and Q-S each vary only area. P-S and T-Q change both area and distance at once, so they cannot separate the two effects.

questions.stem: As the area of an island increases, the number of species generally [Drop-down 1]. As an island's distance from the mainland increases, the number of species generally [Drop-down 2], because fewer new species are able to [Drop-down 3] a far-off island.
questions.rationale: Species rise with area (12 to 25 to 40 as area grows) and fall with distance (12 to 6, 25 to 15) because a wide ocean gap blocks new arrivals. The distractors reverse the trends or the role of isolation.

questions.stem: A student claims, 'Only island size affects how many species live on an island.' Choose the word or phrase that makes each correction of this claim right.
items: The data show that distance from the mainland [ also affects / does not affect ] the number of species.
Comparing islands R and S, which have the same area, the [ closer / farther ] island has more species.
So island size is [ not the only factor / the only factor ] that affects biodiversity.
questions.rationale: Islands R and S share an area of 100 km2, yet the closer one (R, 25 species) beats the farther one (S, 15 species), showing distance matters too. Revising the claim requires recognizing both factors.

stimuli.title: A Limiting Factor At Two Scales
stimuli.phenomenon: Eastern bluebirds nest in holes, called cavities, in old or dead trees. In many woodlands these natural cavities are scarce, so the number of nesting sites can limit how many bluebirds are able to breed. To test this idea, researchers studied two woodlots of different sizes: a small woodlot of 5 hectares and a large woodlot of 25 hectares. First they counted the breeding pairs already nesting in each. Then they put up many artificial nest boxes in both woodlots and counted the breeding pairs again the next spring. In both woodlots, the number of breeding pairs rose sharply after the nest boxes were added, showing that nesting sites had been holding the populations down. The graph shows the number of breeding pairs before and after the nest boxes were added in each woodlot. In the questions that follow, you will use the data to explain how a single limiting factor can control a population at different scales.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Breeding pairs before and after nest boxes were added, in a small and a large woodlot.
figure.title: Breeding Pairs Before and After Adding Nest Boxes

questions.stem: According to the graph, how many breeding pairs were in the large woodlot after nest boxes were added?
questions.rationale: The 'after' bar for the large woodlot reaches 65 pairs. 25 is its 'before' value, 13 is the small woodlot's 'after' value, and 5 is the small woodlot's 'before' value.

questions.stem: Before nest boxes were added, the small woodlot had 5 pairs in 5 hectares and the large woodlot had 25 pairs in 25 hectares, a density of about [Drop-down 1] breeding pair per hectare in each. Because the same limiting factor, the number of [Drop-down 2], controlled both woodlots, the density was about the same at both scales.
questions.rationale: 5 pairs divided by 5 hectares and 25 pairs divided by 25 hectares both give about 1 pair per hectare, and adding nest sites raised both, identifying nest sites as the shared limiting factor. 0.2 inverts the division.

questions.stem: Decide whether each statement about the study is True or False.
rows: Adding nest sites increased the number of breeding pairs in both woodlots.
Nest sites are a limiting factor for this bird population.
The results show that nest sites matter only in the small woodlot.
Before boxes were added, the two woodlots had about the same number of breeding pairs per hectare.
questions.rationale: Both woodlots responded to more nest sites and had the same starting density, so nest sites limit the population at both scales. The false statement wrongly restricts the effect to the small woodlot.

questions.stem: Select all that apply. Which statements are supported by the data?
options: Adding nest sites increased the number of breeding pairs in both woodlots.
Before nest boxes were added, the two woodlots had about the same number of pairs per hectare.
The large woodlot supported more total breeding pairs than the small one.
Nest sites had no effect on the bird population.
Only the large woodlot responded to added nest sites.
questions.rationale: The bars show a rise in both woodlots, equal starting densities, and a larger total in the bigger woodlot. The unselected options contradict the clear increase seen in both woodlots.

standards.pe_text: Construct and revise an explanation based on evidence for the cycling of matter and flow of energy in aerobic and anaerobic conditions.

stimuli.title: Why Peat Piles Up
stimuli.phenomenon: In a well-drained forest, leaves that fall in autumn are usually broken down and gone within a year. Tiny decomposers in the soil use oxygen as they feed on the dead leaves, and most of the carbon returns to the air. In a nearby peat bog, the ground is flooded with water all year, so very little oxygen can reach the soggy, waterlogged soil. Here, decomposers work very slowly, and dead moss and plants pile up year after year without fully breaking down. Over thousands of years these partly decayed remains form thick layers of peat, a build-up of biomass that stores large amounts of carbon. Scientists measured how much leaf material was left after one year in a well-drained soil and in a waterlogged soil. The graph shows their results. In the questions that follow, you will use the evidence to explain how the amount of oxygen in a place affects the cycling of matter and the flow of energy through living things.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Leaf material remaining after one year in two soils.
figure.title: Leaf Material Remaining After One Year

questions.stem: Which result from the graph is the best evidence that a lack of oxygen slows down the breakdown of dead plants?
options: After one year, more leaf material remained in the waterlogged (anaerobic) soil than in the well-drained (aerobic) soil.
After one year, the same amount of leaf material remained in both soils.
After one year, all of the leaf material had broken down in both soils.
After one year, more leaf material remained in the well-drained (aerobic) soil.
questions.rationale: 75% of the leaf mass remained in the low-oxygen waterlogged soil versus only 20% in the oxygen-rich soil, showing that little oxygen slows decomposition. The other options misread the bars or reverse the pattern.

questions.stem: In the well-drained soil, decomposers have plenty of [Drop-down 1], so they break down leaves quickly and carbon returns to the air. In the waterlogged bog this gas is [Drop-down 2], so dead plants build up as peat instead of breaking down.
questions.rationale: Fast (aerobic) decomposition depends on plenty of oxygen; in the flooded bog oxygen is scarce, so decomposers work slowly and biomass accumulates. Sunlight and nitrogen are not the gas that limits decomposition here.

questions.stem: In the well-drained forest, order the steps to show how carbon from a dead leaf cycles back into living things.
items: Carbon is released into the air as carbon dioxide
A dead leaf falls to the forest floor
Plants take in the carbon to build new leaves
Decomposers use oxygen to break down the leaf
questions.rationale: The correct order is: a leaf falls, decomposers use oxygen to break it down, carbon is released as carbon dioxide, and plants take that carbon back in. This completes the cycling of matter through the ecosystem.

questions.stem: Choose the word that makes each prediction correct if the bog were drained so that more oxygen reached the soil.
items: With more oxygen, decomposers would break down the stored peat [ faster / slower ].
Draining the bog would cause the carbon stored in the peat to be released into the air more [ quickly / slowly ].
questions.rationale: Adding oxygen shifts the soil toward aerobic conditions, so decomposers speed up, the biomass breaks down faster, and its stored carbon returns to the air more quickly.

stimuli.title: Pond Oxygen Day And Night
stimuli.phenomenon: A shallow freshwater pond is full of life. Green algae and water plants act as producers, while insects, fish, and tiny decomposers also live in the water. Scientists lowered a sensor into the pond and recorded the amount of dissolved oxygen in the water every three hours for a full day and night. During daylight, the producers use energy from sunlight to make food, and they release oxygen into the water as they do so. After dark, photosynthesis stops, but all the organisms in the pond, including the decomposers breaking down dead material, keep using oxygen. Because of this, the dissolved oxygen climbs during the day, reaches its highest level in the afternoon, and then falls through the night to its lowest point just before dawn. The graph shows how the oxygen level changed. In the questions that follow, you will use the data to explain how producers and decomposers cycle matter and cause oxygen to rise and fall.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Dissolved oxygen in a pond measured over one full day and night.
figure.title: Dissolved Oxygen in a Pond Over 24 Hours

questions.stem: According to the graph, at about what time was the dissolved oxygen highest, and what best explains it?
options: Mid-afternoon, because producers had been adding oxygen through photosynthesis all day.
Just before dawn, because the animals had rested all night.
At midnight, because photosynthesis is fastest in the dark.
At 6 a.m., because oxygen does not change during the day.
questions.rationale: Oxygen peaks near 3 p.m. after a day of photosynthesis by producers. The distractors place the peak in darkness or claim photosynthesis works best at night, which the data contradict.

questions.stem: During the [Drop-down 1], producers use solar energy to make food and release oxygen into the water. After dark, photosynthesis stops, but organisms keep using oxygen, so the dissolved oxygen level [Drop-down 2].
questions.rationale: Producers add oxygen only in daylight, while oxygen use continues around the clock, so oxygen drops at night. Choosing 'night' or 'rises' reverses the daily pattern shown in the data.

questions.stem: Select all that apply. Which observations are evidence that photosynthesis by producers controls the pond's oxygen level?
options: Dissolved oxygen rose from morning to mid-afternoon while it was light.
Dissolved oxygen fell overnight when it was dark.
Dissolved oxygen was lowest just before dawn.
Dissolved oxygen stayed exactly the same all day and night.
The pond contained no algae or water plants.
questions.rationale: Oxygen rising in the light, falling in the dark, and bottoming out before dawn all tie the oxygen level to photosynthesis. A flat line or a pond with no producers would be evidence against that link.

questions.stem: A few cloudy days shade the pond so the producers make much less food and oxygen. Decide whether each prediction is True or False.
rows: The dissolved oxygen in the pond would tend to be lower than on sunny days.
Decomposers would still use oxygen as they break down dead matter.
Carbon would stop cycling and never return to the water or air.
Oxygen in the pond would rise higher than on sunny days.
questions.rationale: Less photosynthesis means less oxygen added, while decomposers keep consuming it, so oxygen drops. Carbon keeps cycling as decomposers release it, so the claims that cycling stops or that oxygen rises higher are false.

stimuli.title: A Dead Zone In The Bay
stimuli.phenomenon: Each summer, part of a coastal bay turns into a 'dead zone,' a region of deep water where dissolved oxygen falls so low that fish and crabs must swim away or die. The trouble begins when rain washes fertilizer and other nutrients into the bay. The extra nutrients feed an enormous bloom of algae, which are producers, near the sunlit surface. When these algae die, they sink to the bottom in huge amounts. There, decomposers break down the dead algae and use up the oxygen in the deep water faster than it can be replaced. Where the oxygen runs out, breakdown slows and almost no animals can survive. Scientists lowered an oxygen sensor from the surface to the bottom and recorded the dissolved oxygen at each depth. The graph shows their measurements. In the questions that follow, you will use the evidence to explain how the supply of oxygen controls where matter is broken down and carbon is returned to the water.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Dissolved oxygen at increasing water depth in the bay during summer. Water below about 2 mg/L cannot support most fish.
figure.title: Dissolved Oxygen vs. Depth in the Bay

questions.stem: According to the graph, at about what depth does the dissolved oxygen first drop below 2 mg/L, low enough to form a dead zone?
options: 4 m
6 m
8 m
questions.rationale: Oxygen is still 5 mg/L at 6 m but has fallen to about 1.8 mg/L at 8 m, so 8 m is where it first drops below 2. 12 m is also low but is not the first depth to cross the threshold.

questions.stem: Arrange the steps that create the summer dead zone in the order they happen, from first to last.
items: The algae die and sink to the bottom.
Extra nutrients wash into the bay.
Oxygen becomes so low that fish and crabs leave or die.
Algae grow into a huge bloom of producers.
Decomposers use up the oxygen as they break down the dead algae.
questions.rationale: Nutrients arrive, algae bloom, the algae die and sink, decomposers consume the oxygen, and finally the low oxygen drives animals out. Reordering the decomposers before the algae die breaks the cause-and-effect chain.

questions.stem: Match each part of the bay to what happens there.
questions.optset: producers make food and release oxygen / decomposers break down dead matter quickly using oxygen / breakdown is slow and few animals can survive
correct: producers make food and release oxygen
decomposers break down dead matter quickly using oxygen
breakdown is slow and few animals can survive
questions.rationale: Producers work in the light near the surface, decomposition is fast where oxygen is plentiful, and where oxygen runs out breakdown slows and animals cannot live. Mismatches show confusion about how oxygen controls each zone.

questions.stem: Choose the word that makes each prediction correct if fewer nutrients washed into the bay.
items: If fewer nutrients washed into the bay, the algae bloom would be [ smaller / larger ].
With less dead algae to break down, decomposers would use [ less / more ] oxygen at the bottom.
As a result, the low-oxygen dead zone would likely [ shrink / grow ].
questions.rationale: Fewer nutrients mean a smaller bloom, less dead algae to decompose, less oxygen used up, and therefore a smaller dead zone. Choosing 'larger,' 'more,' or 'grow' reverses this cause-and-effect chain.

standards.pe_text: Use mathematical representations to support claims for the cycling of matter and flow of energy among organisms in an ecosystem.

stimuli.title: Energy In Silver Springs
stimuli.phenomenon: Silver Springs is a large freshwater spring ecosystem in Florida. In the 1950s, ecologist Howard Odum measured how much energy was stored each year by the living things at each trophic level of this ecosystem. He measured energy in kilocalories per square meter per year (kcal/m2/yr). The producers, mostly water plants and algae that capture solar energy, stored by far the most energy, about 20,810 kcal/m2/yr. The primary consumers that ate the plants stored about 3,368 kcal/m2/yr. The secondary consumers, which ate the plant-eaters, stored only about 383, and the top predators stored just 21. At every step up the food chain, most of the energy was used for life processes or lost as heat, so far less energy was left for the next level. The graph shows the energy stored at each trophic level. In the questions that follow, you will use the data to describe how energy flows through the trophic levels of this ecosystem.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Energy stored each year at each trophic level in Silver Springs, Florida.
figure.title: Energy Stored at Each Trophic Level

questions.stem: According to the graph, which trophic level stores the most energy each year?
options: Producers
Primary consumers
Secondary consumers
Top predators
questions.rationale: Producers store about 20,810 kcal/m2/yr, far more than any other level. The amount of stored energy drops at each higher level, so the top predators store the least (21).

questions.stem: The primary consumers stored about 3,368 kcal/m2/yr, while the producers stored about 20,810 kcal/m2/yr. The primary consumers stored roughly [Drop-down 1] of the energy stored by the producers. This shows that as energy moves up to the next trophic level, the amount of stored energy [Drop-down 2].
questions.rationale: 3,368 divided by 20,810 is about 0.16, or roughly 16%, so only a small fraction of the producers' energy is stored by the next level. Because most energy is used or lost as heat, stored energy decreases at each step. '84%' is the fraction lost, not passed on.

questions.stem: Select all of the statements that are supported by the data in the graph.
options: Each higher trophic level stores less energy than the one below it.
Most of the energy captured by the producers never reaches the top predators.
The top predators store more energy than the producers.
At each step, only a small fraction of the energy passes to the next trophic level.
Energy increases as it moves up the food chain.
questions.rationale: Stored energy falls from 20,810 to 3,368 to 383 to 21, so each level stores less, only a small fraction (roughly a tenth or less) reaches the next level, and little of the producers' energy reaches the top. The false options reverse this flow.

questions.stem: Match each organism from a freshwater spring to its trophic level.
rows: Insects that eat the water plants
Small fish that eat the insects
Large bass that eat the small fish
questions.optset: producer / primary consumer / secondary consumer / top predator
questions.rationale: Plants and algae make their own food (producers), the insects that eat them are primary consumers, the small fish that eat the insects are secondary consumers, and the bass at the end of the chain are the top predators. This identifies the organisms that make up each level of the energy pyramid.

stimuli.title: Ten Percent Up The Chain
stimuli.phenomenon: Energy enters most ecosystems as sunlight and is captured by producers, then passes from one living thing to the next as organisms are eaten. In a grassland, grass captures energy from the Sun. Grasshoppers eat the grass, shrews eat the grasshoppers, and owls eat the shrews. Ecologists can measure how much energy is stored each year by the living things at each of these trophic levels, in kilocalories per square meter per year. When they do, they find that a large amount of energy is stored by the grass, but far less is stored at each higher level. Most of the energy at each level is used for the organisms' life processes or lost to the surroundings as heat, so only a small part is left to pass on to the next level. The table shows the energy stored at each trophic level of this grassland food chain. In the questions that follow, you will use the data to describe how energy flows through the trophic levels.

figure.caption: Table 1. Energy stored each year at each trophic level of a grassland food chain.

questions.stem: According to the table, which trophic level stores the least energy each year?
options: Producers (grass)
Primary consumers (grasshoppers)
Secondary consumers (shrews)
Top predators (owls)
questions.rationale: The owls store only 10 kcal/m2/yr, the smallest value in the table. Energy drops at each step up, so the top predators are left with the least.

questions.stem: The grasshoppers store about [Drop-down 1] of the energy stored by the grass. At each step up the chain, only about [Drop-down 2] of the energy is passed on; the rest is used for life processes or lost as heat.
questions.rationale: 1,000 divided by 10,000 is about 0.10, or 10%, so roughly one-tenth of the energy moves to the next level. Choosing 100% or 'all' ignores the energy used up or lost as heat at each level.

questions.stem: Arrange the organisms in order from the one that stores the most energy to the one that stores the least.
items: Shrews (secondary consumers)
Grass (producers)
Owls (top predators)
Grasshoppers (primary consumers)
questions.rationale: Stored energy falls from grass (10,000) to grasshoppers (1,000) to shrews (100) to owls (10), so the order is grass, grasshoppers, shrews, owls. This is the shape of an energy pyramid.

questions.stem: Decide whether each statement about the food chain is True or False.
rows: Each higher trophic level stores about one-tenth as much energy as the level just below it.
Because so little energy reaches the top, there is enough for only a few owls.
Most of the energy captured by the grass never reaches the owls.
Energy increases as it moves up the food chain.
questions.rationale: The tenfold drop at each step means little energy reaches the top, supporting few owls, and most of the grass's energy is used or lost before reaching them. Energy decreases, not increases, up the chain.

stimuli.title: Why Top Predators Are Few
stimuli.phenomenon: In the open ocean, tiny floating algae called phytoplankton are the producers that capture energy from sunlight. Zooplankton, small drifting animals, eat the phytoplankton. Small fish eat the zooplankton, and large tuna eat the small fish. Scientists can measure the biomass at each level, which is the total mass of all the living things of that type in a given area, reported in grams per square meter. When the biomass is measured, a clear pattern appears: there is a great deal of phytoplankton, much less zooplankton, still less mass of small fish, and only a tiny mass of tuna. So little of the matter and energy at each level is built into the level above it that the top of the food chain can support only a small number of large predators. The graph shows the biomass at each trophic level. In the questions that follow, you will use the data to explain why biomass shrinks up the levels and why top predators are few.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Biomass at each trophic level of an ocean food chain.
figure.title: Biomass at Each Trophic Level

questions.stem: According to the graph, which group has the greatest biomass?
options: Phytoplankton (producers)
Zooplankton
Small fish
Tuna
questions.rationale: The phytoplankton bar reaches 500 g/m2, taller than every other bar. As the producers at the base of the chain, they hold the most biomass.

questions.stem: Select all that apply. Which ideas help explain why there are so few tuna (top predators) in this ecosystem?
options: Only a small part of the energy at each level is passed on to the next level.
Biomass gets smaller at each higher trophic level.
Each tuna must eat many smaller fish to get enough energy.
There is more biomass at the top of the chain than at the bottom.
The producers (phytoplankton) have the least biomass of any level.
questions.rationale: Little energy reaching each higher level, shrinking biomass, and the many prey each tuna needs all explain the small number of top predators. The unselected options contradict the pyramid shown in the data.

questions.stem: Match each organism to its trophic level.
questions.optset: producer / primary consumer / secondary consumer / top predator
questions.rationale: Phytoplankton make their own food (producers), zooplankton eat them (primary consumers), small fish eat the zooplankton (secondary consumers), and tuna at the end of the chain are the top predators. This identifies the levels of the biomass pyramid.

questions.stem: Choose the number or word that makes each statement correct.
items: The producers' biomass (500 g/m2) is about [ 250 / 25 ] times the tuna biomass (2 g/m2).
This shows that biomass [ shrinks / grows ] as you move up the trophic levels.
Because so little energy reaches the top level, top predators must be [ few / many ].
questions.rationale: 500 divided by 2 is 250, so the producers' biomass dwarfs the tuna's. Biomass shrinks up the levels, and the small amount reaching the top means top predators must be few.

standards.pe_text: Develop a model to illustrate the role of photosynthesis and cellular respiration in the cycling of carbon among the biosphere, atmosphere, hydrosphere, and geosphere.

stimuli.title: Carbon Cycling and the Keeling Curve
stimuli.phenomenon: High on the Mauna Loa volcano in Hawaii, instruments have measured the amount of carbon dioxide (CO2) in the air since 1958, far from cities and factories. The record shows two clear patterns. First, the average amount of CO2 rises year after year. Second, within each year the level falls a little every northern-hemisphere summer and climbs again each winter. The summer dip happens because vast numbers of green producers across North America, Europe, and Asia carry out photosynthesis during the growing season, pulling CO2 out of the atmosphere. In fall and winter, plants drop their leaves and decomposers and other organisms release CO2 back through cellular respiration. Meanwhile, burning coal, oil, and natural gas moves carbon that was locked in the geosphere for millions of years into the air. In the questions that follow, you will use the data and your knowledge of the carbon cycle to explain how carbon moves among Earth's spheres.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Average yearly atmospheric carbon dioxide measured at Mauna Loa Observatory, Hawaii.
figure.title: Atmospheric CO2 at Mauna Loa
figure.source: Data: NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory, Mauna Loa Observatory.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the long-term pattern in the data from 1960 to 2023, and what it shows about carbon?
options: The average CO2 level rose steadily, showing that carbon is entering the atmosphere faster than producers remove it.
The average CO2 level stayed about the same, showing that carbon is perfectly balanced among the spheres.
The average CO2 level fell steadily, showing that producers are removing more carbon than is added.
The average CO2 level rose and then fell back to its 1960 value.
questions.rationale: The curve climbs from about 317 to 421 ppm, so more carbon is being added to the atmosphere than producers pull out. Choosing 'balanced' or 'fell' misreads the clear upward trend.

questions.stem: Each northern-hemisphere summer, the amount of CO2 in the air falls. This happens because producers carry out [Drop-down 1], which moves carbon from the atmosphere into the [Drop-down 2]. Later, when organisms and decomposers carry out [Drop-down 3], carbon returns to the atmosphere.
dd: cellular respiration | photosynthesis | fossil fuel formation
questions.rationale: Photosynthesis by producers pulls atmospheric carbon into living tissue (the biosphere); cellular respiration by organisms and decomposers releases it back. Reversing the two processes is the common misconception this item targets.

questions.stem: Place the steps in order to trace one carbon atom as it cycles from the atmosphere, through living things, and back to the atmosphere.
items: A consumer eats the producer and takes in the carbon.
Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere is taken in by a producer during photosynthesis.
The carbon returns to the atmosphere as CO2.
The producer uses the carbon to build sugars and body tissue.
Consumers and decomposers release the carbon through cellular respiration.
questions.rationale: Correct order: atmospheric CO2 is fixed by a producer through photosynthesis, the carbon is built into tissue, a consumer eats the producer, then consumers and decomposers release the carbon by respiration, returning it to the atmosphere.

questions.stem: Select all of the changes that would tend to increase the long-term amount of CO2 in the atmosphere.
options: Burning more coal and oil, moving carbon from the geosphere into the air
Clearing and burning large areas of forest
Planting large new forests that grow for many decades
Reducing the number of producers that carry out photosynthesis
questions.rationale: Burning fossil fuels and forests releases stored carbon, and fewer producers means less CO2 removed by photosynthesis. Planting long-lived forests instead pulls carbon out of the air, so it is not selected.

stimuli.title: Where Earth Stores Its Carbon
stimuli.phenomenon: Carbon is found in every part of the Earth system, but it is not spread evenly. It is held in the atmosphere as carbon dioxide gas, in the ocean as dissolved carbon, on land in living plants and in the soil, and deep underground in coal, oil, and natural gas. Scientists call each of these a carbon reservoir, or store, and each store belongs to one of Earth's spheres. Carbon does not stay in one place. Producers pull carbon dioxide out of the air and build it into their tissue, consumers and decomposers release it again, and the ocean surface both takes in and gives off the gas. Burning coal and oil moves carbon that was locked away for millions of years back into the air. The table lists the amount of carbon held in four reservoirs, in gigatons (billions of tons). In the questions that follow, you will use the data to describe how carbon is stored in and cycled among Earth's spheres.

figure.caption: Table 1. Estimated carbon stored in four reservoirs and the sphere each belongs to (representative values, in gigatons of carbon).
rows: Living plants and soil on land

questions.stem: According to the table, which carbon reservoir holds the most carbon?
options: Carbon dioxide in the air (atmosphere)
Dissolved carbon in the ocean (hydrosphere)
Living plants and soil on land (biosphere)
Coal, oil, and natural gas (geosphere)
questions.rationale: The ocean holds about 38,000 gigatons, far more than any other reservoir in the table. Students who pick the atmosphere or fossil fuels are choosing a much smaller store.

questions.stem: Match each process to the way it moves carbon between Earth's spheres.
rows: Cellular respiration by animals and decomposers
Ocean surface taking in the gas
questions.optset: Atmosphere to biosphere / Biosphere to atmosphere / Geosphere to atmosphere / Atmosphere to hydrosphere
questions.rationale: Photosynthesis moves carbon from the air into living things, respiration and decomposition return it to the air, burning fossil fuels moves long-buried carbon from the geosphere to the air, and the ocean surface takes carbon dioxide from the air into the water.

questions.stem: Decide whether each statement about carbon and the spheres is True or False.
rows: The carbon in a plant's leaves came from carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
Photosynthesis and cellular respiration together move carbon between the atmosphere and the biosphere.
Carbon stored in coal and oil can never move into any other sphere.
Once carbon enters the ocean, no process can ever return it to the air.
questions.rationale: Producers build atmospheric carbon into their tissue, and photosynthesis and respiration continually exchange carbon between the air and living things. Fossil fuels release carbon to the air when burned, and the ocean surface both absorbs and releases carbon dioxide, so neither store is permanent.

questions.stem: Select all of the changes that would move carbon out of a living or buried store and add carbon dioxide to the atmosphere.
options: Burning large amounts of coal and oil
Clearing and burning a forest
A large increase in ocean plants that take in carbon dioxide
Decomposers breaking down a huge amount of dead plant material
Planting forests that grow for many years
questions.rationale: Burning fossil fuels and forests, and decomposition of dead matter, all release stored carbon to the air. Growing more ocean plants or planting long-lived forests pulls carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere instead, so those are not selected.

stimuli.title: When a Rainforest Is Cleared
stimuli.phenomenon: A patch of tropical rainforest holds a large amount of carbon. Over many years, the trees act as producers, taking in carbon dioxide from the air and using it to build wood, leaves, and roots; more carbon is stored in the rich soil below. When the forest is cleared to make farmland, the trees are usually cut and burned, and the bare soil begins to break down. Burning the wood and the decay of the dead roots release the stored carbon back into the air as carbon dioxide. A field of crops or grass holds far less carbon than the forest did, so much of the carbon that was locked in the living forest ends up in the atmosphere. Researchers estimated the carbon stored on one hectare of land while it was forest and again years after it became farmland. The graph shows the results for two carbon stores. In the questions that follow, you will use the data to explain how clearing a forest shifts carbon among Earth's spheres.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Carbon stored per hectare in living plants and in soil, as forest and as cleared farmland (representative values).
figure.title: Carbon Stored per Hectare: Forest vs. Farmland

questions.stem: Based on the graph, how does the carbon stored in living plants change when forest becomes farmland?
options: It stays about the same.
It increases greatly.
It decreases greatly, from about 180 to about 8 tons per hectare.
It drops to exactly zero.
questions.rationale: The living-plant bar falls from about 180 tons per hectare in forest to about 8 tons in farmland, a large decrease but not all the way to zero. The soil store changes much less.

questions.stem: Place the steps in order (1 = first) to show how carbon moves as a forest is cleared and burned.
items: The carbon is released into the air as carbon dioxide.
Trees take in carbon dioxide from the air and build it into wood and leaves.
The cleared land, now farmland, holds much less carbon than the forest did.
The trees are cut down and burned.
questions.rationale: Carbon first enters the forest when trees take in carbon dioxide and build tissue; clearing and burning then release that stored carbon to the air, and the farmland left behind holds far less carbon than the forest did.

questions.stem: Choose the word that makes each statement about the carbon shift correct.
items: Before clearing, most of the forest's carbon was stored in the [ biosphere / geosphere ].
Burning the trees moves that carbon into the [ atmosphere / hydrosphere ].
This shift happens because burning and decay [ release / absorb ] carbon dioxide.
questions.rationale: The living forest is part of the biosphere; burning and decay release its stored carbon as carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. Choosing 'absorb' or the wrong sphere reverses the direction of the carbon shift.

questions.stem: Suppose the cleared land is allowed to grow back into forest over many years. As the new trees grow, they would take in carbon dioxide through [Drop-down 1], moving carbon from the atmosphere back into the [Drop-down 2]. Over time, the amount of carbon stored on the land would [Drop-down 3].
questions.rationale: Growing producers pull carbon dioxide from the air through photosynthesis and store it in living tissue, returning carbon to the biosphere and raising the carbon stored on the land. This reverses the shift caused by clearing.

standards.pe_text: Evaluate the claims, evidence, and reasoning that the complex interactions in ecosystems maintain relatively consistent numbers and types of organisms in stable conditions, but changing conditions may result in a new ecosystem.

stimuli.title: Wolves Return to Yellowstone
stimuli.phenomenon: Gray wolves were killed off in Yellowstone National Park by the 1920s, and for seventy years the park had no wolves. During that time, large numbers of elk grazed freely along streams and browsed young willow and aspen shoots down to the ground. Streamside trees stayed short, and beavers, which need willow for food and dam building, nearly disappeared. In 1995, biologists reintroduced gray wolves to the park. Over the next twenty years, researchers tracked the wolves, the elk herd, the number of beaver colonies, and the height of streamside willows. As wolves became established, elk numbers dropped and elk avoided lingering in open streamside areas. Willows and aspens along many streams grew taller, and beaver colonies increased. Some scientists describe this as a chain of effects that reshaped the whole streamside community. In the questions that follow, you will evaluate the claim, evidence, and reasoning that returning one predator shifted this ecosystem toward a new, more diverse state.

figure.caption: Table 1. Northern Yellowstone gray wolves, elk, beaver colonies, and streamside willow height after wolf reintroduction (representative monitoring values).

questions.stem: Which claim is best supported by the data in the table?
options: Returning wolves reduced elk numbers and grazing, which allowed willows and beaver colonies to recover, shifting the streamside ecosystem.
Returning wolves fed directly on willows, which is why willow height increased.
The growing elk herd caused biologists to remove wolves from the park.
Willow height increased first, and this caused the wolf population to grow.
questions.rationale: As wolves rose, elk fell, and willows and beavers recovered, matching a predator-driven chain of effects. Wolves do not eat willow, elk did not grow, and willow did not increase before the wolves returned.

questions.stem: Select all of the trends in the table that support the claim that the ecosystem shifted after wolves were reintroduced.
options: Gray wolves increased from 21 to about 100.
Elk dropped from about 17,000 to about 6,000.
Beaver colonies increased from 1 to 11.
Streamside willow height increased from 0.5 m to 2.4 m.
Elk numbers increased as the wolf population grew.
questions.rationale: The rise in wolves, drop in elk, and recovery of beavers and willows are all consistent with a shifted ecosystem. The last option states the opposite of what the data show and is therefore not evidence for the claim.

questions.stem: Decide whether each statement is True or False.
rows: Before wolves returned, large numbers of elk kept streamside willows short by overgrazing.
Taller willows provided the food and material that let beaver colonies increase.
Wolves increased willow height mainly by feeding on willow plants themselves.
The data prove that this new state will remain unchanged no matter how conditions change in the future.
questions.rationale: Overgrazing by abundant elk explains the earlier short willows, and recovering willows support beavers. Wolves affect willows indirectly through elk, not by eating willow, and no data set can prove permanent stability, since extreme future disturbances could shift the system again.

questions.stem: A student claims the table alone proves that wolves caused the willows to recover. This claim is [Drop-down 1], because the data were collected over the same years in which other conditions could also have changed. The claim would be [Drop-down 2] by separate records showing that rainfall and temperature stayed about the same during this period. The single most useful additional evidence would be [Drop-down 3].
dd: too strong as stated | fully proven | impossible to judge
willow growth in nearby areas that still have no wolves | the color of the wolves | the number of park visitors
correct: willow growth in nearby areas that still have no wolves
questions.rationale: A single correlated data set cannot rule out other causes, so the claim is too strong; steady climate records would strengthen it by removing a rival explanation, and a wolf-free comparison area would be the strongest additional test.

stimuli.title: Sea Otters and the Kelp Forest
stimuli.phenomenon: Along the rocky coasts of the northern Pacific, giant kelp grows in dense underwater 'forests' that shelter many kinds of fish and other animals. Sea urchins graze on kelp, chewing through the stalks that hold it to the seafloor. Sea otters are one of the few predators that eat large numbers of sea urchins. For many years fur hunters removed sea otters from long stretches of coast. Scientists compared these coasts with nearby coasts where otters were still common. Where otters were present, urchins were few and kelp forests were thick and full of life. Where otters were absent, urchins were extremely abundant and had grazed the kelp down to bare rock, leaving a lifeless zone called an 'urchin barren.' The table compares representative measurements from the two kinds of coast. In the questions that follow, you will evaluate the claim, evidence, and reasoning that sea otters keep the kelp-forest ecosystem in a stable state.

figure.caption: Table 1. Representative measurements from Pacific coasts with sea otters present and with sea otters absent.

questions.stem: Which claim is best supported by the data in the table?
options: Where sea otters are present, they keep urchin numbers low, so kelp forests stay thick and full of life.
Sea otters feed directly on kelp, which is why kelp is more abundant where otters live.
Sea urchins protect kelp forests from being overgrazed.
The number of kelp stalks is the same whether or not otters are present.
questions.rationale: Otter coasts have few urchins and abundant kelp, while otter-free coasts have many urchins and almost no kelp, supporting the claim that otters control urchins and keep the kelp forest stable. Otters eat urchins, not kelp, and the kelp counts clearly differ between coasts.

questions.stem: Match each organism to its role in the kelp-forest ecosystem.
questions.optset: Producer / Grazer that eats kelp / Predator that eats urchins
questions.rationale: Kelp is the producer, urchins are the grazers that eat it, and otters are the predators that eat urchins. Knowing these roles is needed to trace how a change at one level affects the others.

questions.stem: Place the events in order (1 = first) to show what happens along a coast after sea otters are removed.
items: The kelp forest disappears, leaving bare rock called an urchin barren.
Sea otters are removed from the coast by hunters.
With few predators, the sea urchin population grows very large.
The large number of urchins graze the kelp down to the seafloor.
questions.rationale: Removing the predator lets urchins multiply, and the abundant urchins overgraze the kelp until the forest becomes a barren. This chain shows how the loss of one species can push the ecosystem into a very different state.

questions.stem: Choose the word that makes each statement correct.
items: Where otters are present, urchin numbers stay [ low / high ], so the kelp forest remains stable.
Removing the otters is a [ large / small ] change that the kelp forest cannot absorb.
This change pushes the community into a [ new / unchanged ] state, the urchin barren.
questions.rationale: A healthy otter population holds urchins in check and keeps the system stable, but removing the top predator is a disturbance large enough to flip the community into a new, kelp-free state. Choosing 'small' or 'unchanged' misses that losing a key species can transform the ecosystem.

stimuli.title: Wolves and Moose on Isle Royale
stimuli.phenomenon: Isle Royale is a large, isolated island in Lake Superior. Since the late 1950s, scientists have counted its wolves and moose each year, in one of the longest studies of a predator and its prey. For many years the two populations rose and fell in linked cycles but stayed within a fairly consistent range. When moose were abundant, wolves had plenty of food and increased; the larger wolf population then reduced the moose herd, after which wolf numbers fell again. This kept both populations fluctuating around a relatively stable balance. Then extreme disturbances struck. Around 1980 a disease accidentally brought to the island by humans killed most of the wolves, and years later a series of unusually harsh winters sharply cut the moose herd. The table shows representative counts for selected years. In the questions that follow, you will evaluate claims, evidence, and reasoning about what keeps this island ecosystem stable and what can push it to change.

figure.caption: Table 1. Representative counts of wolves and moose on Isle Royale in selected years.

questions.stem: For many years before 1980, which statement best describes the wolf and moose populations?
options: They rose and fell in linked cycles but stayed within a fairly consistent range.
Both populations grew larger every single year.
Both populations disappeared completely.
The two populations changed in ways that had nothing to do with each other.
questions.rationale: The predator and prey cycled up and down together around a relatively stable balance, which is the pattern of a stable ecosystem. The populations neither grew without limit nor were unconnected.

questions.stem: Select all of the observations in the table that are evidence of an extreme disturbance to the ecosystem.
options: Wolves dropped from about 50 in 1980 to about 14 in 1982.
Moose dropped from about 1,100 in 1995 to about 500 in 1997.
Wolves numbered about 20 in 1970 and about 16 in 1995.
Moose numbered about 1,050 in 1970 and about 1,100 in 1995.
questions.rationale: The sharp wolf crash after 1980 and the sharp moose crash after 1995 are large, sudden changes tied to disease and harsh winters. The other two comparisons show numbers staying within their usual range, which is evidence of stability, not disturbance.

questions.stem: Place the steps in order (1 = first) to show one turn of the cycle that kept the populations balanced.
items: With more food, the wolf population increases.
The moose population grows large.
The larger wolf population reduces the moose herd.
With less food, the wolf population falls again.
questions.rationale: Abundant moose give wolves plenty of food, so wolves increase; the larger wolf population then cuts the moose herd, which later leaves wolves with less food, so wolves decline. This feedback keeps both populations fluctuating around a balance.

questions.stem: Decide whether each statement about stability and change on the island is True or False.
rows: The linked cycles show that complex interactions can keep populations relatively consistent over time.
The wolf crash after 1980 shows that an extreme disturbance can push a population far outside its usual range.
Because the ecosystem was stable for decades, the data prove it can never be changed by any future event.
A single harsh winter and a normal year would be expected to affect the moose herd equally.
questions.rationale: Long-term cycling is evidence of a stable system, and the disease-driven wolf crash shows an extreme disturbance can break that stability, but no data can prove permanent stability, and an extreme harsh winter affects the herd far more than a normal year. Recognizing the false statements shows students can judge reasoning about modest versus extreme disturbance.

standards.pe_text: Design, evaluate, and refine a solution for reducing the impacts of human activities on the environment and biodiversity.

stimuli.title: Zebra Mussels in the Pipes
stimuli.phenomenon: Zebra mussels are small, striped shellfish native to lakes in Eastern Europe and Asia. In the 1980s they were carried to the North American Great Lakes in the ballast water of cargo ships, an introduced species with no natural predators in their new home. They reproduce quickly and attach in thick layers to any hard surface, including the inside of the large pipes that draw lake water into power plants and drinking-water treatment plants. As mussel layers build up, they narrow the pipes and slow the flow of water, forcing utilities to shut down and clean the pipes at great cost. The mussels also filter enormous volumes of water, removing the tiny plankton that native fish and mussels depend on. A city water utility must choose a way to keep its intake pipes clear while limiting further harm to the lake's living things. In the questions that follow, you will analyze and evaluate possible solutions to this problem.

figure.caption: Table 1. Four proposed solutions for keeping water-intake pipes clear of zebra mussels.
rows: Scrape and clean pipes on a schedule

questions.stem: Place the steps in order to complete the cause-and-effect chain that explains how zebra mussels create a problem for the water utility.
items: The thick layers narrow the pipes and slow the water flow.
Zebra mussels arrive in ballast water and spread through the lake.
The utility must shut down and clean the pipes, raising costs.
Mussels attach in layers to the inside of water-intake pipes.
questions.rationale: Correct order: the mussels arrive and spread, attach inside the pipes, build up layers that slow the flow, and finally force costly shutdowns for cleaning.

questions.stem: Match each proposed solution to its main trade-off or drawback.
rows: Scrape and clean pipes on a schedule
questions.optset: Harms native fish and mussels / High installation cost / Labor-intensive and must be repeated / Does not stop tiny larvae
questions.rationale: Chlorine is effective but toxic to native species; the coating is low-risk but expensive; scheduled scraping is cheap but must be redone repeatedly; fine screens are cheap but let microscopic larvae pass and settle downstream.

questions.stem: The utility sets these requirements: the solution must keep the pipes clear, must not add chemicals that harm native species, and must fit a limited budget. Based on the table, which solution best meets all three requirements?
options: Add chlorine to intake water
Coat pipes with anti-attachment material
Scrape and clean pipes on a schedule
Install fine mesh intake screens
questions.rationale: Scheduled scraping is low cost, low risk to native species, and at least moderately effective, so it meets all three requirements. Chlorine fails the no-harm criterion, the coating fails the budget constraint, and the screens fail the clear-pipes criterion.

questions.stem: Suppose the utility instead decides to add chlorine to the intake water. Based on the table, the intake pipes would likely become [Drop-down 1], but the number of native fish and mussels near the outflow would likely [Drop-down 2], because chlorine is [Drop-down 3].
dd: harmful to many aquatic organisms | a nutrient for plankton | harmless to all life
questions.rationale: Chlorine is highly effective, so pipes clear, but the table lists its risk to native species as high because chlorine is toxic to many aquatic organisms, so native populations near the outflow would likely fall.

stimuli.title: Shrinking a Coastal Dead Zone
stimuli.phenomenon: Every spring, rivers carry fertilizer washed off farm fields into a coastal bay. The fertilizer is rich in nitrogen and phosphorus, the same nutrients that make crops grow. In the bay, these nutrients feed an enormous bloom of algae. When the algae die, decomposers use up the oxygen in the water as they break the algae down. The result is a 'dead zone,' a large area of water so low in oxygen that fish, crabs, and shellfish cannot survive there. Local officials want to shrink the dead zone by reducing the amount of fertilizer that reaches the bay, without putting the region's farms out of business. Engineers and farmers have proposed several possible solutions, each with different costs, benefits, and drawbacks. The table lists four options and how they compare. In the questions that follow, you will analyze and evaluate solutions for reducing the impact of fertilizer runoff on the bay.

figure.caption: Table 1. Four proposed solutions for reducing fertilizer runoff into the bay.
rows: Plant buffer strips of plants along rivers
Restore wetlands to filter the water

questions.stem: Based on the information, what directly causes the low oxygen in the dead zone?
options: Decomposers use up the oxygen as they break down the huge amount of dead algae.
The fertilizer itself removes oxygen from the water.
Fish breathe out all of the oxygen in the bay.
Cold river water cannot hold any oxygen.
questions.rationale: The nutrients feed an algal bloom; when the algae die, decomposers consume the water's oxygen, creating the dead zone. The fertilizer triggers the bloom but does not remove oxygen itself.

questions.stem: Match each proposed solution to its main trade-off or drawback.
questions.optset: May reduce the crop yield / Only a medium reduction in runoff / High cost to build and maintain / Very high cost
correct: Only a medium reduction in runoff
High cost to build and maintain
questions.rationale: Each solution helps but carries a cost: using less fertilizer may cut yields, buffer strips remove less runoff, wetland restoration is costly, and treatment plants are the most expensive. Weighing these trade-offs is central to choosing a design.

questions.stem: The officials want a solution that shrinks the dead zone but keeps farms in business. Select all of the criteria and constraints a good solution should meet.
options: It should clearly reduce the amount of fertilizer reaching the bay.
It should not force the region's farms out of business.
It should raise as much fertilizer runoff as possible.
It should have a cost the community can afford.
It should completely stop all farming near the bay.
questions.rationale: A workable solution must reduce runoff (the goal), stay affordable, and keep farms operating (the key constraint). Increasing runoff or shutting down all farming would fail the officials' requirements.

questions.stem: Decide whether each prediction about a solution is True or False.
rows: If farmers use less fertilizer, less nitrogen and phosphorus will reach the bay.
Restoring wetlands would help because wetlands can filter nutrients out of the water before it reaches the bay.
Reducing the fertilizer that reaches the bay would make the algal bloom larger.
Choosing the treatment plants would have no drawbacks at all.
questions.rationale: Cutting nutrient runoff shrinks the bloom and the dead zone, and wetlands filter nutrients, so both help. Reducing nutrients cannot enlarge the bloom, and the very high cost of treatment plants is a real drawback, so those statements are false.

stimuli.title: Controlling the Kudzu Vine
stimuli.phenomenon: Kudzu is a fast-growing vine brought to the southeastern United States long ago to control soil erosion. With no natural enemies in its new home, it became an aggressive invasive species. Kudzu can grow up to a foot a day, blanketing trees, fences, and even buildings. As it piles leaves on top of native plants, it blocks their sunlight, and the smothered plants die. Over time a kudzu-covered hillside loses most of its native plants and the animals that depended on them, so the area's biodiversity falls. A county park district wants to clear kudzu from a natural area and keep it from spreading, without harming the native plants it is trying to protect. Workers have suggested several methods, each with different costs and drawbacks. The table lists four options. In the questions that follow, you will analyze and evaluate solutions for reducing the impact of this invasive vine on the natural area.

figure.caption: Table 1. Four proposed methods for controlling kudzu in a natural area.
rows: Dig out every root crown by hand

questions.stem: Based on the information, how does kudzu most directly cause native plants to die?
options: It blankets them and blocks the sunlight they need.
It poisons the soil so nothing else can grow.
It eats the native plants for food.
It scares away the animals that pollinate them.
questions.rationale: Kudzu piles leaves over other plants and blocks their sunlight, so the shaded native plants die. It is a plant and does not poison the soil or eat other plants.

questions.stem: Place the steps in order (1 = first) to complete the cause-and-effect chain of how kudzu harms the natural area.
items: Native plants die and the animals that depended on them decline.
Kudzu is introduced to an area that has no natural enemies for it.
The fast-growing vine blankets native plants and blocks their sunlight.
The kudzu spreads quickly and covers the hillside.
questions.rationale: The vine arrives with no natural enemies, spreads and covers the land, blocks the sunlight native plants need, and the loss of those plants causes the animals that relied on them to decline. This chain lowers the area's biodiversity.

questions.stem: Suppose the park district chooses to spray a strong weed killer. Based on the table, the kudzu would likely be controlled [Drop-down 1], but the number of native plants near the sprayed area might [Drop-down 2], because the table lists this method's risk to native plants as [Drop-down 3].
dd: decrease | increase | stay exactly the same
questions.rationale: The weed killer is highly effective on kudzu, but the table rates its risk to native plants as high, so spraying it could also kill nearby native plants and reduce their numbers. This trade-off is the drawback of the most effective chemical option.

questions.stem: The park district wants a method that is effective, affordable, and safe for native plants. Choose the word or phrase that makes each statement correct.
items: Spraying strong weed killer is effective but fails the requirement to be [ safe for native plants / affordable ].
Digging out every root by hand is safe and effective but fails the requirement to be [ affordable / effective ].
Compared with those two, repeated mowing best [ balances / ignores ] all three requirements.
questions.rationale: Weed killer harms native plants, hand-digging costs too much, and mowing is low-cost, low-risk, and moderately effective, so it best balances the criteria and constraints. Evaluating these trade-offs is how a design solution is judged.

standards.pe_text: Evaluate the evidence for the role of group behavior on individual and species’ chances to survive and reproduce.

stimuli.title: Why Emperor Penguins Huddle
stimuli.phenomenon: Emperor penguins raise their chicks during the Antarctic winter, the coldest breeding conditions of any bird. Each male balances a single egg on his feet for about two months in temperatures near -40 degrees C and fierce winds, and during this whole time he cannot leave to eat. To keep warm, thousands of males pack tightly together into dense huddles. Penguins on the freezing outer edge slowly shuffle toward the warmer center, and those in the middle move outward, so the group constantly rotates and each bird takes a turn in the protected core. Researchers measured how much body mass and energy penguins lost, the body temperature they kept, and how many eggs hatched, comparing birds that huddled with birds that stayed apart. The results let us test whether this cooperative behavior actually helps individuals and the species. In the questions that follow, you will evaluate the evidence that huddling improves each penguin's chance to survive and reproduce.

figure.caption: Table 1. Measurements from male emperor penguins that huddled versus those that stayed apart during the Antarctic winter.

questions.stem: Which claim about huddling is best supported by all four measurements in the table?
options: Huddling lowers a penguin's energy use and body-mass loss and raises hatching success, helping it survive and reproduce.
Huddling raises a penguin's energy use but keeps it warmer, so it is not worth the cost.
Huddling helps penguins stay warm but has no effect on how many eggs hatch.
Huddling only benefits the penguins in the cold outer edge of the group.
questions.rationale: Huddling birds lose less mass, use less energy, stay warmer, and hatch twice as many eggs, supporting a clear survival and reproduction benefit. The other options each contradict at least one row of the data.

questions.stem: Sort each inference by how the data in the table treat it.
rows: Huddling penguins lose less body mass each day than penguins that stay apart.
Huddling lowers the share of eggs that successfully hatch.
Huddling penguins live longer after winter than penguins that stay apart.
Huddling penguins keep a higher body temperature.
questions.optset: Supported by the data / Contradicted by the data / Not enough data
questions.rationale: Mass loss and body temperature are directly measured and favor huddling; hatching data contradict the claim that huddling lowers hatching; the table has no post-winter lifespan data, so that inference cannot be judged.

questions.stem: Choose the word that makes each statement correct.
items: Penguins in a huddle use [ less / more ] energy than penguins that stay apart.
Using less energy lets a fasting penguin survive [ longer / shorter ] without food.
These results show a survival [ benefit / cost ] of cooperative group behavior.
questions.rationale: The table shows huddling birds use fewer energy units and lose less mass, so a fasting penguin can last longer on its stored fat, which is a clear energy benefit of cooperative behavior.

questions.stem: Select all of the additional pieces of evidence that would help test the claim that huddling improves survival and reproduction.
options: The percentage of huddling and solitary penguins that survive the entire winter
The number of chicks successfully raised by huddling versus solitary parents
Whether penguins that spend more time in the warm center survive the winter better than those on the edge
The color pattern of each penguin's feathers
questions.rationale: Winter survival rates and chicks raised directly test survival and reproduction, and time spent in center versus edge shows whether the benefit is shared across the group. Feather color is unrelated to the claim.

stimuli.title: Meerkats on Guard Duty
stimuli.phenomenon: Meerkats are small, social mammals that live in groups in the deserts of southern Africa. While most of the group digs for insects and other food, one meerkat often stops feeding, climbs to a high spot, and acts as a 'sentinel,' scanning the sky and ground for hawks, jackals, and snakes. If the sentinel spots danger, it gives a sharp alarm call, and the whole group dashes to the safety of a burrow. Group members take turns on guard, so no single meerkat bears the cost of watching all the time. Researchers compared foraging groups that had a sentinel on duty with groups that had no sentinel. They recorded how often a predator caught a group by surprise, how many members were lost, how much time the animals spent feeding, and how many pups the group raised. The table shows representative results. In the questions that follow, you will evaluate the evidence that this group behavior improves each meerkat's chance to survive and reproduce.

figure.caption: Table 1. Representative results for meerkat groups foraging with and without a sentinel on guard.
rows: Pups raised per group per year

questions.stem: Which claim is best supported by all four measurements in the table?
options: Having a sentinel lowers predator attacks and losses and raises feeding time and pups raised, helping the meerkats survive and reproduce.
Having a sentinel makes no difference to how many meerkats are caught.
Having a sentinel helps the group feed but leads to fewer pups.
Having a sentinel only helps the one meerkat standing guard.
questions.rationale: Groups with a sentinel have far fewer attacks and losses, feed more, and raise twice as many pups, supporting a clear survival and reproduction benefit. Each other choice contradicts at least one row of the data.

questions.stem: Select all of the patterns in the table that support the idea that having a sentinel helps the group survive and reproduce.
options: Groups with a sentinel had fewer surprise attacks (2 versus 9 per month).
Groups with a sentinel lost fewer members to predators (1 versus 5 per year).
Groups with a sentinel spent less time feeding than groups without one.
Groups with a sentinel raised more pups (6 versus 3 per year).
questions.rationale: Fewer attacks, fewer losses, and more pups all support a survival and reproduction benefit. The feeding-time statement is false because guarded groups actually fed more, not less, so it is not evidence and is not selected.

questions.stem: Use the data to complete a summary. Meerkat groups with a sentinel had [Drop-down 1] surprise attacks and raised [Drop-down 2] pups than groups without a sentinel. Overall, the data show that having a sentinel [Drop-down 3] the group.
dd: fewer | more | the same number of
more | fewer | the same number of
benefits | harms | has no effect on
questions.rationale: Summarizing the table, guarded groups had fewer attacks and raised more pups, so the sentinel behavior benefits the group. The distractors contradict the values in the table.

questions.stem: Decide whether the data in the table support each inference. Mark True if the data support it and False if the data do not.
rows: Having a sentinel lowers the number of meerkats caught by predators.
Having a sentinel lowers the number of pups the group raises.
Meerkats stand guard less often when a hawk is nearby.
Groups with a sentinel spend more of the day feeding.
questions.rationale: The table supports lower predator losses and more feeding time, contradicts the claim that guarding lowers pups (it raises them), and says nothing about how hawks change guarding, so that inference is not supported. Sorting inferences this way tests whether each is backed by the evidence.

stimuli.title: Division of Labor in a Hive
stimuli.phenomenon: A honeybee colony can contain tens of thousands of bees, yet only one queen lays eggs. The rest are female workers that do different jobs, and a worker's job changes as she ages. Young workers act as nurses inside the hive, feeding the queen and the developing larvae. Slightly older workers build wax comb and store incoming food. Older workers guard the entrance, and the oldest leave the hive as foragers, gathering nectar and pollen to feed the whole colony. Because the jobs are divided among many specialized workers, the colony can feed its young, defend itself, and store food all at the same time. Researchers compared colonies with a normal mix of worker jobs to colonies in which the balance of jobs was disturbed. The table shows representative results. In the questions that follow, you will evaluate the evidence that dividing work among group members improves the colony's chance to survive and reproduce.

figure.caption: Table 1. Representative results for honeybee colonies with a normal division of labor and with a disturbed division of labor.

questions.stem: Which claim is best supported by the data in the table?
options: A normal division of labor helps the colony store more food, raise more workers, and survive the winter better.
Dividing the work among specialized bees has no effect on the colony.
Colonies with a disturbed division of labor store more food.
Only the queen's behavior affects whether the colony survives.
questions.rationale: Colonies with a normal division of labor stored more than twice the food, raised more than twice the workers, defended better, and survived winter far more often, supporting a clear benefit. The other choices contradict the data.

questions.stem: Place the steps in order (1 = first) to show how dividing the work helps the colony reproduce.
items: The colony raises many new workers and stores plenty of food.
Different workers specialize in nursing, building, guarding, and foraging.
With food stored and young raised, the colony survives the winter and can produce new colonies.
All of the colony's needs are met at the same time.
questions.rationale: Specialized workers let the colony meet all of its needs at once, so it raises many workers and stores food, which lets it survive the winter and produce new colonies. This chain links the group behavior to survival and reproduction.

questions.stem: Sort each inference by how the data in the table treat it.
rows: A normal division of labor helps the colony store more food.
A disturbed division of labor raises more new workers.
Colonies with a normal division of labor produce more queens each year.
A normal division of labor improves the colony's chance of surviving winter.
questions.optset: Supported by the data / Contradicted by the data / Not enough data
questions.rationale: Food stored and winter survival are directly measured and favor a normal division of labor; the worker-raising data contradict the second inference; and the table has no data on queens produced, so that inference cannot be judged.

questions.stem: A researcher wants to test whether a normal division of labor also improves the colony's ability to reproduce. Complete the plan. The most useful additional evidence would be the number of [Drop-down 1] each colony produces. The [Drop-down 2] would be the least useful evidence. The claim would be best supported if colonies with a normal division of labor produced [Drop-down 3].
dd: new colonies (swarms) | wax cells in the comb | flowers in the field
color painted on the outside of the hive | number of new colonies | amount of food stored
more new colonies | fewer new colonies | the same number of colonies
correct: color painted on the outside of the hive
