questions.rationale: Reproduction in honeybees means producing new colonies, so counting new swarms is the key evidence and more swarms would support the claim. The color painted on the hive has nothing to do with reproduction, so it is the least useful evidence.

standards.pe_text: Ask questions to clarify relationships about the role of DNA and chromosomes in coding the instructions for characteristic traits passed from parents to offspring.

stimuli.title: Inheriting the Milk-Digesting Trait
stimuli.phenomenon: Nearly all humans carry the gene that codes for lactase, the protein that breaks down the sugar in milk. Whether a person keeps making lactase into adulthood depends on a single gene that has two forms, called alleles. The allele for lactase persistence (L) is dominant, and the allele for non-persistence (l) is recessive. A person who cannot digest milk as an adult stops producing lactase and feels ill after drinking it. The table shows one family in which both parents can digest milk as adults. Three of their four children can also digest milk, but one child cannot. The alleles that code for this trait are carried on chromosomes and passed from parents to offspring during fertilization. In the questions that follow, you will use the family data to explain how alleles on chromosomes determine whether milk can be digested and to predict how the trait is passed to offspring.

figure.caption: Table 1. Ability to digest milk as an adult for members of one family.
columns: Can Digest Milk as an Adult?

questions.stem: A scientist wants to investigate how the ability to digest milk is passed from parents to offspring. Which question could best be answered by studying inheritance in families like the one shown?
options: How many glasses of milk does each family member drink per day?
What alleles must each parent carry if one of their children cannot digest milk?
How does the taste of milk change when it is left out overnight?
At what age do most people stop drinking milk?
questions.rationale: A testable inheritance question focuses on the alleles parents carry and pass to offspring; the distractors ask about behavior or the chemistry of milk, which cannot reveal how the trait is inherited.

questions.stem: Place the steps in order to complete a cause-and-effect chain showing how a chromosome determines whether an offspring can digest milk.
items: The offspring's pair of alleles (genotype) determines whether lactase is produced.
A gene carried on a chromosome holds the coded instructions, or allele, for the milk-digesting trait.
Whether the person can digest milk (the phenotype) is expressed as the trait.
During fertilization, one allele from each parent combines in the zygote.
questions.rationale: The correct order is: an allele on a chromosome carries the instructions, alleles from each parent combine at fertilization, the resulting genotype determines lactase production, and the phenotype (able or unable to digest milk) is then expressed.

questions.stem: Match each genotype to the phenotype it produces for the milk-digesting trait.
questions.right: Ability to Digest Milk as an Adult
questions.optset: Can digest milk / Cannot digest milk
questions.rationale: Because L is dominant, both LL and Ll produce lactase and can digest milk; only the homozygous recessive ll cannot. Choosing 'cannot' for Ll reveals a misunderstanding of dominance.

questions.stem: Both parents can digest milk, but one of their children cannot. This shows that both parents have the genotype Ll. If these parents have another child, what is the probability that the child will NOT be able to digest milk as an adult?
questions.rationale: A cross of Ll x Ll produces LL, Ll, Ll, and ll, so 1 in 4 (25%) offspring are ll and cannot digest milk. Choosing 50% confuses the ll fraction with the heterozygous fraction; 75% is the fraction that CAN digest milk.

stimuli.title: Tracing a Widow's Peak
stimuli.phenomenon: A widow's peak is a V-shaped point where the hairline dips down in the center of the forehead. Whether a person has a widow's peak or a straight hairline is influenced mainly by a single gene with two alleles. The allele for a widow's peak (W) is dominant, and the allele for a straight hairline (w) is recessive. These alleles are carried on chromosomes and passed from parents to offspring at fertilization. The pedigree in Table 1 follows one family across three generations. In generation I, the grandmother and grandfather both have a widow's peak. They had several children, including the uncle (generation II), who has a widow's peak, and the mother (generation II), who has a straight hairline. The mother's partner, the father, married into the family and also has a straight hairline. In generation III, the mother and father's two children both have straight hairlines. In the questions that follow, you will use the pedigree to explain how alleles on chromosomes determine the hairline trait and to predict how it is passed to offspring.

figure.caption: Table 1. Hairline trait for members of one family across three generations.

questions.stem: The grandmother and grandfather both have a widow's peak, yet their daughter (the mother) has a straight hairline. Which conclusion is best supported by the pedigree?
options: The widow's-peak allele is recessive to the straight-hairline allele.
Each grandparent carries one widow's-peak allele and one hidden straight-hairline allele.
The mother has a straight hairline even though neither grandparent carries a straight-hairline allele.
The grandparents must each carry two straight-hairline alleles.
questions.rationale: A straight-hairline child (ww) must receive a w allele from each parent, so both widow's-peak grandparents are Ww, each carrying a hidden recessive allele; the widow's-peak allele is dominant. Option C ignores that the recessive allele must have been carried, and D contradicts the grandparents having widow's peaks.

questions.stem: Complete the cause-and-effect chain showing how genetic material determines the mother's hairline. The hairline gene is carried on a [Drop-down 1]. The mother received one hairline [Drop-down 2] from each parent at [Drop-down 3]. Her two alleles together make up her [Drop-down 4], which determines the hairline she shows (her phenotype).
questions.rationale: Genes sit on chromosomes; at fertilization each parent contributes one allele; the pair of alleles is the genotype, which determines the phenotype. Replication copies DNA but does not combine alleles from two parents, so it is the wrong choice for the third blank.

questions.stem: Match each family member to what the pedigree shows about their genotype for the hairline gene (W = widow's-peak allele, w = straight-hairline allele).
questions.optset: must be Ww / must be ww / could be WW or Ww
questions.rationale: The grandfather has a widow's peak but a straight-hairline (ww) child, so he must carry a w allele and is Ww. The mother's straight hairline means she is ww. The uncle has a widow's peak with no straight-hairline child shown, so his genotype cannot be pinned down: WW or Ww.

questions.stem: The mother (straight hairline) and father (straight hairline) could have more children. Decide whether each prediction is True or False.
rows: Any additional child of this couple is expected to have a straight hairline.
This couple could have a child with a widow's peak.
If the daughter in generation III later has children with a partner whose genotype is WW, those children could have a widow's peak.
questions.rationale: Two straight-hairline (ww) parents can pass only w alleles, so all their children are ww and have straight hairlines; a widow's peak requires a W allele this couple cannot provide. A WW partner, however, would give every child a W allele, producing a widow's peak.

stimuli.title: Roan Coat Color in Cattle
stimuli.phenomenon: In Shorthorn cattle, coat color is controlled by a single gene with two alleles. One allele (written C^R) makes red hairs, and the other (C^W) makes white hairs. Neither allele masks the other; they are codominant. A calf with two red alleles (C^R C^R) has a fully red coat, and a calf with two white alleles (C^W C^W) has a fully white coat. A calf that inherits one of each (C^R C^W) grows a coat with red and white hairs mixed together, a color ranchers call roan. The alleles sit on chromosomes and are passed to each calf at fertilization. One rancher first bred red cattle with white cattle, and every calf was roan. The rancher then bred those roan cattle with one another and recorded many more calves. Table 1 shows the coat colors from both crosses. In the questions that follow, you will use the data to explain how codominant alleles on chromosomes determine coat color and to predict the coats of future calves.

figure.caption: Table 1. Coat colors of calves from two Shorthorn cattle crosses.

questions.stem: In the first cross (red x white), what was the coat color of every calf?
options: Fully red
Fully white
Roan (red and white hairs mixed)
Half the calves red and half white
questions.rationale: Red (C^R C^R) crossed with white (C^W C^W) can produce only C^R C^W calves. Because the two alleles are codominant, each of these calves shows both red and white hairs and is roan. The table confirms all 32 calves were roan.

questions.stem: Choose the word that makes each statement about coat color correct.
items: A roan calf shows both red and white hairs because both of its alleles are [ expressed / hidden ].
Because both alleles appear separately in the coat instead of blending into one new shade, this pattern is [ codominance / incomplete dominance ].
A fully white calf must have inherited [ two / one ] white allele(s).
questions.rationale: In codominance both alleles are fully expressed and appear separately (distinct red and white hairs), rather than blending to an intermediate shade as in incomplete dominance. A fully white coat requires two C^W alleles.

questions.stem: Place the steps in order (1 = first) to show how a calf's coat color is determined.
items: The calf's two alleles together make up its genotype, such as C^R C^W.
A coat-color gene is carried on a chromosome, as an allele for red (C^R) or an allele for white (C^W).
The genotype is expressed as the calf's coat color, its phenotype.
At fertilization, the calf receives one coat-color allele from each parent.
questions.rationale: The chain runs: an allele on a chromosome carries the instruction, the calf receives one allele from each parent at fertilization, the two alleles form the genotype, and the genotype is expressed as the coat-color phenotype.

questions.stem: Select all statements that correctly predict the calves expected from crossing a roan bull (C^R C^W) with a white cow (C^W C^W).
options: About half of the calves are expected to be roan.
About half of the calves are expected to be fully white.
About one quarter of the calves are expected to be fully red.
No calf is expected to have a fully red coat.
All of the calves are expected to be roan.
questions.rationale: Roan (C^R C^W) crossed with white (C^W C^W) yields half C^R C^W (roan) and half C^W C^W (white). A fully red coat needs two C^R alleles, but the white parent can pass only C^W, so no calf can be fully red and not all calves are roan.

standards.pe_text: Make and defend a claim based on evidence that inheritable genetic variations may result from: (1) new genetic combinations through meiosis, (2) viable errors occurring during replication, and/or (3) mutations caused by environmental factors.

stimuli.title: Sources of Variation Among Chicks
stimuli.phenomenon: A research team sequenced the same 10 genes in a pair of zebra finches and in each of their five chicks. Most differences among the chicks came from new combinations of the alleles the two parents already carried, because each chick received a different mix of the mother's and father's alleles. In addition, every chick carried a few new DNA changes, called variants, that were found in neither parent. These new variants appeared as single base changes (substitutions) or as inserted or deleted bases. One chick that developed under extra ultraviolet (UV) light in the nest carried far more new variants than its siblings. The table shows, for each chick, whether it received a new combination of the parents' alleles, how many new variants it carried that neither parent had, and its UV exposure. In the questions that follow, you will use the data to make and support a claim about the sources of inheritable genetic variation.

figure.caption: Table 1. Sources of genetic difference for five chicks of the same two parents.

questions.stem: Which claim about the source of the chicks' genetic variation is best supported by the data for all five chicks?
options: The chicks vary only because they inherited different combinations of their parents' alleles.
The chicks vary only because of new variants caused by UV light.
The chicks vary because they inherited new combinations of parental alleles and because new variants arose that neither parent carried.
The chicks do not differ genetically from their parents.
questions.rationale: Every chick shows both a new allele combination and at least one new variant, so both sources act. The single-source options ignore part of the data, and the last option contradicts the presence of new variants.

questions.stem: Select all statements that are supported by the data in the table.
options: Every chick received a new combination of its parents' alleles.
Every chick carried at least one new variant found in neither parent.
The chick exposed to extra UV light carried the most new variants.
New variants were found in only one of the five chicks.
The five chicks are genetically identical to one another.
questions.rationale: The first three statements match the columns in the table. 'Only one chick' contradicts the variant counts, and 'genetically identical' contradicts both the new combinations and the differing variant counts.

questions.stem: Match each source of inheritable genetic variation to the evidence in this study that best shows it.
rows: Mutation caused by an environmental factor
questions.optset: Each chick has a unique mix of the parents' alleles / A new variant appears in a chick with no outside cause / The chick under extra UV light carries the most new variants
correct: Each chick has a unique mix of the parents' alleles
A new variant appears in a chick with no outside cause
The chick under extra UV light carries the most new variants
questions.rationale: New allele mixes come from recombination; a spontaneous new variant with no external cause points to a replication error; extra new variants tied to UV exposure point to an environmentally caused mutation.

questions.stem: Decide whether each statement about passing these variations to the next generation is True or False.
rows: A new variant will be passed to a chick's own offspring only if it is present in that chick's egg or sperm cells.
A new combination of the parents' alleles can be inherited by the chick's offspring.
A DNA change that occurs only in a chick's skin cells will be passed to that chick's offspring.
questions.rationale: Only variation carried in the egg or sperm (sex cells) is heritable. Recombined allele combinations in the sex cells can be passed on, but a change limited to somatic cells such as skin cells cannot.

stimuli.title: Why Littermates Differ
stimuli.phenomenon: Two pet rabbits, a mother and a father, have a litter of six baby rabbits, called kits. Even though every kit has the same two parents, no two kits are exactly alike. A small part of the difference comes from brand-new DNA changes, but most of it comes from something else. Each parent carries two different versions, called variants, of many of their genes. When sex cells (eggs and sperm) form, only one variant of each gene goes into each sex cell, and the variants are shuffled into a new mix each time. As a result, every kit inherits its own combination of the parents' variants. Scientists examined three of the mother's genes, one affecting fur length, one affecting ear length, and one affecting whisker length, and recorded which of her two variants (labeled 1 or 2) each kit received. Table 1 shows the results. In the questions that follow, you will use the data to make and support a claim about why offspring of the same two parents are not identical.

figure.caption: Table 1. Variant of each gene (1 or 2) that each kit inherited from the mother.

questions.stem: According to the table, do any two kits have exactly the same combination of variants for all three genes?
options: No; each kit has its own unique combination of variants.
Yes; all six kits share the same combination.
Yes; Kit 5 and Kit 6 have the same combination.
The table does not give enough information to tell.
questions.rationale: Comparing the three-gene pattern in each row shows all six kits differ; Kit 5 (1,1,1) and Kit 6 (2,2,2) are in fact opposites. Each kit received a different mix of the mother's variants.

questions.stem: Complete the claim about why the kits differ. Most of the differences among the kits come from new [Drop-down 1] of the variants their parents already carried, not from brand-new DNA changes. Because the mother carries two variants of each of the three genes and passes one of each, the number of different variant combinations she could give a kit is [Drop-down 2]. This shuffling of variants happens as her [Drop-down 3] form.
dd: sex cells | skin cells | red blood cells
questions.rationale: Siblings differ mainly because the parents' existing variants are recombined into new combinations. With two choices at each of three genes there are 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 possible combinations; the distractor 6 is the number of kits and 3 is the number of genes. The shuffling occurs as sex cells form.

questions.stem: Select all statements that are supported by the data and the information given.
options: Each of the six kits received a unique combination of the mother's variants.
The differences among the kits come mainly from new combinations of variants the parents already had.
The six kits are genetically identical to one another.
Each kit's variants were created by a brand-new mutation in that kit.
The same two parents can produce kits with many different variant combinations.
questions.rationale: The table shows six unique combinations from the same two parents, supporting new combinations (recombination) as the main source of the differences. The kits are not identical, and their variants were inherited and reshuffled, not newly mutated in each kit.

questions.stem: Choose the word or phrase that makes each statement correct.
items: These new variant combinations can be passed to the next generation because they are carried in the rabbits' [ sex cells / fur cells ].
If two of these kits later become parents, their own offspring will again inherit [ new combinations / identical copies ] of variants.
New combinations of variants add to the [ heritable / temporary ] variation in the rabbit population.
questions.rationale: Variation carried in sex cells is heritable, so each new generation is reshuffled into new combinations of the parents' variants, adding to the heritable variation present in the population.

stimuli.title: A New Wing Color Appears
stimuli.phenomenon: A biologist studies a large population of small beetles in which every beetle has a green wing case. One summer, a single beetle hatches with a blue wing case, a color never before seen in this population. To find out where the blue color came from, the biologist reads a short section of the pigment-gene DNA in the blue beetle and in both of its green parents. The two parents have the usual DNA sequence, but the blue beetle carries a single changed base (a substitution) that neither parent has. This brand-new variant, or allele, was not inherited from the parents; it appeared as a new change in the DNA. Because the change is also present in the blue beetle's sex cells, the blue beetle can pass it to its offspring. Table 1 compares the DNA sequences. In the questions that follow, you will use this evidence to explain how a new mutation can add a brand-new heritable variation to a population.

figure.caption: Table 1. A short section of the pigment-gene DNA in the blue beetle and its two parents.

questions.stem: According to Table 1, how does the blue beetle's DNA compare with the DNA of its two parents?
options: It is identical to both parents' DNA.
It has a single changed base that neither parent has.
It is missing the entire pigment gene.
It matches the father's DNA but not the mother's.
questions.rationale: Both parents read ...ACA... while the blue beetle reads ...AAA..., a single-base substitution found in neither parent. This changed base is evidence of a new change in the DNA, not something inherited from a parent.

questions.stem: Match each source of new genetic variation to the description that fits it.
questions.optset: a brand-new DNA change, such as the blue beetle's substitution, found in neither parent / a new mix of variants the parents already carried / a change that is carried in sex cells and can be passed to offspring
correct: a brand-new DNA change, such as the blue beetle's substitution, found in neither parent
a new mix of variants the parents already carried
a change that is carried in sex cells and can be passed to offspring
questions.rationale: The blue beetle's substitution, absent from both parents, is a new mutation; recombination instead produces a new mix of variants the parents already carried; and any change is heritable only when it is present in sex cells. This distinguishes the two sources of variation from the condition for heritability.

questions.stem: Place the events in order (1 = first) to show how the new blue variant can enter and spread in the population.
items: A beetle inherits the new variant and hatches with a blue wing case.
A new change appears in the DNA of one of a green parent's sex cells.
Over several generations, more beetles carry the blue variant.
The blue beetle passes the new variant to some of its own offspring.
questions.rationale: The mutation first arises in a parent's sex cell; the offspring that inherits it hatches blue; that beetle passes the variant to its own offspring; and over several generations the variant becomes more common in the population.

questions.stem: Decide whether each statement about the evidence is True or False.
rows: Comparing the parents' DNA with the offspring's DNA is useful evidence for showing that the blue variant is new.
If the DNA change were found only in the blue beetle's wing (body) cells and not its sex cells, it could still be passed to its offspring.
Sequencing the DNA of more green beetles in the population would help show whether the blue variant was truly absent before.
questions.rationale: Comparing parent and offspring sequences shows the change is new. Only changes present in sex (germ-line) cells are heritable, so a change limited to body cells would not pass on. Sequencing more beetles is additional evidence about whether the variant was already present.

standards.pe_text: Apply concepts of statistics and probability to explain the variation and distribution of expressed traits in a population.

stimuli.title: Blood-Type Distribution in a Population
stimuli.phenomenon: Human ABO blood type is controlled by a single gene that has three alleles. The I^A and I^B alleles are codominant, and the i allele is recessive. A person's genotype produces one of four phenotypes: type A, type B, type AB, or type O. Blood type is set entirely by which alleles a person inherits; unlike traits such as height, it is not changed by diet or other environmental factors. A blood bank recorded the blood types of 2,000 volunteer donors from one region. The bar graph shows the percentage of donors with each blood type. Type O was the most common and type AB the least common, but the exact mix of types differs from one population to another. In the questions that follow, you will read the distribution, use probability to predict the blood types of offspring, and explain how genotype produces the observed variation of this trait in the population.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Percentage of 2,000 blood donors with each ABO blood type.
figure.title: Blood-Type Distribution in 2,000 Donors

questions.stem: According to the graph, which blood type is the most common in this group of donors, and about what percentage of donors have it?
options: Type O, about 45%
Type A, about 45%
Type AB, about 11%
Type O, about 4%
questions.rationale: The tallest bar is type O at about 45%. The distractors either mislabel the tallest bar as type A or pair type O with the wrong value.

questions.stem: Select all statements that are supported by the graph and the information given.
options: Type AB is the least common blood type in this group.
More donors have type A than type B.
A person's blood type can change if they change their diet.
Type O and type A together make up most of the donors.
Every population has exactly the same mix of blood types.
questions.rationale: AB has the shortest bar, A (40%) exceeds B (11%), and O plus A (85%) is most of the donors. Diet does not change blood type, and the passage states the mix differs among populations, so those two statements are false.

questions.stem: Choose the word that makes each statement about this trait correct.
items: Because a person with type AB blood expresses both the I^A and I^B alleles, these alleles are [ codominant / recessive ].
A person with type O blood must have inherited [ two / one ] i allele(s), so their genotype is homozygous.
Reading the graph from most common to least common gives the order O, A, B, [ AB / B ].
questions.rationale: Type AB shows both alleles expressed, which defines codominance; type O is genotype ii, requiring two recessive i alleles; and the least common type in the distribution is AB.

questions.stem: One parent has genotype I^A i (type A) and the other has genotype I^B i (type B). Using a Punnett square, the probability that a child of these parents will have type O blood is [Drop-down 1], and the probability that a child will have type AB blood is [Drop-down 2].
questions.rationale: A cross of I^A i x I^B i gives four equally likely genotypes: I^A I^B (AB), I^A i (A), I^B i (B), and ii (O). Type O requires two i alleles (25%) and type AB requires both I^A and I^B (25%).

stimuli.title: Variation in Adult Height
stimuli.phenomenon: Height is a continuous trait: adults are not simply 'tall' or 'short' but fall along a smooth range of heights. Unlike blood type, which is set by a single gene, adult height is influenced by many different genes acting together and also by environmental factors such as childhood nutrition. Because so many small factors add together, most people end up near the middle of the range, while fewer are found at the very short or very tall ends. A researcher measured the height of 1,000 adult women in one region and sorted the measurements into 5-centimeter intervals. When the number of women in each interval is graphed, the bars form a symmetrical, bell-shaped distribution centered near the average height. Figure 1 shows the results. In the questions that follow, you will use basic statistics and the shape of this distribution to describe how a trait shaped by many genes and the environment varies across a population.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Number of women in each height interval, from a sample of 1,000 adult women.
figure.title: Distribution of Adult Height

questions.stem: According to Figure 1, which height interval contains the greatest number of women?
questions.rationale: The tallest bar, 300 women, is the 165-169 cm interval at the center of the distribution. The bars fall off symmetrically on either side of this peak.

questions.stem: Complete the description of the distribution. The graph is nearly [Drop-down 1] around its center and shaped like a [Drop-down 2]. The average (mean) height lies near the [Drop-down 3] of the range, and [Drop-down 4] of the women are near the middle than at the extremes.
dd: symmetrical | tilted to one side | flat
questions.rationale: The counts rise to a single central peak and fall off evenly, so the distribution is symmetrical and bell-shaped, the mean sits near the middle of the range, and more individuals cluster near the mean than in the tails.

questions.stem: Select all statements that help explain why adult height varies smoothly across a wide range instead of falling into just a few separate groups.
options: Height is influenced by many genes acting together.
Environmental factors such as childhood nutrition also affect height.
Height is controlled by a single gene with only two alleles.
Because many small factors add together, most people fall near the middle of the range.
A person's height is determined only by their blood type.
questions.rationale: A continuous, bell-shaped trait results from many genes plus environmental influences adding together, which places most individuals near the middle. A single two-allele gene would give only a few discrete groups, and blood type is unrelated to height.

questions.stem: Decide whether each statement about this population is True or False.
rows: If better childhood nutrition raised the height of everyone in the region, the whole distribution could shift toward greater heights.
A woman measured at 196 cm would fall far in the right tail, well outside the range where most women lie.
Because height is a continuous trait, we would expect it to sort into exactly four groups, like ABO blood type.
questions.rationale: Because environment affects height, improving nutrition can shift the whole distribution upward. A 196 cm measurement lies far above the bulk of the data, an outlier in the tail. A continuous trait does not sort into a few discrete classes the way a single-gene trait like blood type does.

stimuli.title: Flower Color in Pea Plants
stimuli.phenomenon: In pea plants, flower color is controlled by a single gene with two alleles. The allele for purple flowers (P) is dominant, and the allele for white flowers (p) is recessive. A plant has purple flowers if it carries at least one P allele (genotype PP or Pp) and white flowers only if it carries two p alleles (pp). A gardener grew a large plot of pea plants from seeds made by crossing many heterozygous purple plants (Pp) with one another. When the plants bloomed, the gardener counted 792 plants with purple flowers and 258 with white flowers. Flower color here depends only on the alleles a plant inherits; sunlight and soil did not change the colors. Figure 1 shows the trait distribution. In the questions that follow, you will read this trait distribution and use a Punnett square to predict the probability of flower colors from a single cross.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Number of pea plants with purple and with white flowers in the plot.
figure.title: Flower-Color Distribution in the Plot

questions.stem: According to Figure 1, which flower color is more common, and about what ratio of purple to white does the plot show?
options: Purple is more common, at about 3 purple to 1 white.
White is more common, at about 3 white to 1 purple.
Purple is more common, at about 1 purple to 1 white.
White is more common, at about 2 white to 1 purple.
questions.rationale: 792 purple to 258 white is close to a 3:1 ratio, so purple is about three times as common as white. This is the pattern expected from crossing heterozygous (Pp) plants.

questions.stem: Choose the word that makes each statement about genotype and phenotype correct.
items: A white-flowered pea plant must have the genotype [ pp / PP ].
A purple-flowered plant carries at least [ one / zero ] P allele(s).
Among the purple plants from this Pp x Pp cross, [ most / none ] are heterozygous (Pp).
questions.rationale: White is recessive and requires two p alleles (pp); purple requires at least one P allele. In a Pp x Pp cross the purple offspring are 1 PP to 2 Pp, so most purple plants (about two-thirds) are heterozygous.

questions.stem: The gardener crosses two heterozygous purple plants (Pp x Pp). Using a Punnett square, the probability that an offspring will have purple flowers is [Drop-down 1], and the probability that it will have white flowers is [Drop-down 2].
questions.rationale: A Pp x Pp cross gives genotypes 1 PP : 2 Pp : 1 pp. Three of four offspring (75%) carry at least one P allele and are purple, while one of four (25%) is pp and white.

questions.stem: Decide whether each statement about the white-flowered plants is True or False.
rows: In this Pp x Pp cross, white-flowered plants are an expected outcome, not a rare anomaly.
About 1 out of every 4 offspring of a Pp x Pp cross is expected to have white flowers.
The 258 white plants out of 1,050 total are far outside the number expected from a 3:1 ratio.
questions.rationale: Recessive white plants are the expected 1-in-4 outcome of a Pp x Pp cross, so they are not anomalies. One quarter of 1,050 is about 263, so the observed 258 white plants match the expected 3:1 ratio closely rather than being outliers.

standards.pe_text: Communicate scientific information that common ancestry and biological evolution are supported by multiple lines of empirical evidence.

stimuli.title: Multiple Clues to Common Ancestry
stimuli.phenomenon: Nearly every living thing, from yeast to fish to humans, builds a protein called cytochrome c that helps cells release energy. Scientists can read the order of the amino acid building blocks in this protein and count how many of them differ from the human version. They can also compare the bones in animal limbs, study the order in which body structures form in early embryos, and examine where fossils sit in layers of rock. When these separate lines of evidence are compared, they often point to the same pattern of relationships among species. Table 1 shows how many amino acids in cytochrome c differ from the human protein in several organisms. In the questions that follow, you will use this table and other lines of evidence to explain how they support the idea that these species share common ancestors.

figure.caption: Table 1. Number of amino acid differences in cytochrome c compared with the human protein.
figure.source: Data: cytochrome c amino acid sequence comparisons (Dickerson, 1972).
columns: Amino acid differences from human cytochrome c

questions.stem: Based only on Table 1, which organism shares the most recent common ancestor with humans?
options: Chimpanzee
Horse
Tuna
Yeast
questions.rationale: The chimpanzee has the fewest amino acid differences (0), indicating the closest relationship and most recent common ancestor. Choosing yeast (44 differences) reverses the pattern and treats more differences as closer kinship.

questions.stem: Select all statements that are supported by the evidence.
options: Species with fewer amino acid differences in cytochrome c are more closely related to humans.
The chimpanzee is more closely related to humans than the tuna is.
A larger number of amino acid differences means two species are more closely related.
Comparing embryos and fossils can provide evidence about relationships in addition to protein and DNA comparisons.
Cytochrome c is found only in humans and chimpanzees.
questions.rationale: A, B, and D are supported: fewer amino-acid differences means a closer relationship, the chimpanzee is closer to humans than the tuna, and embryos and fossils add independent evidence. C reverses the relationship; E is false (cytochrome c is found in nearly all organisms).

questions.stem: Match each line of evidence to what scientists compare when they use it.
questions.optset: Order of nucleotides in genes / Arrangement of bones in limbs / Order in which body structures appear before birth / Position of remains in rock layers
correct: Order in which body structures appear before birth
Position of remains in rock layers
questions.rationale: Each independent line of evidence examines a different feature: nucleotide order (DNA), limb bone arrangement (anatomy), timing of structures in embryos (embryology), and layering of remains (fossils). Together these separate lines support common ancestry.

stimuli.title: Same Bones, Different Jobs
stimuli.phenomenon: A human arm reaches and grasps, a whale's flipper pushes it through water, a bat's wing lifts it into the air, and a cat's front leg carries it as it runs. On the outside these forelimbs look nothing alike and do very different jobs. Yet when scientists look inside, they find the same set of bones arranged in the same pattern: one long upper bone, a pair of lower bones, a cluster of wrist bones, and several digits. Body parts that share this kind of matching structure are called homologous structures. Scientists also notice that whales carry a pair of tiny hip and hind-limb bones buried in their bodies that are far too small to help them swim. These reduced, leftover parts are called vestigial structures. The table compares the forelimb bones of four mammals. In the questions that follow, you will use these anatomical patterns as evidence to explain how these animals can share a common ancestor.

figure.caption: Table 1. Forelimb structure of four mammals with very different ways of moving.

questions.stem: According to the table, what do the forelimbs of all four mammals have in common?
options: They all perform the same job.
They are all built from the same set and arrangement of bones.
They each contain a different number of upper-arm bones.
They are all exactly the same size.
questions.rationale: Every row lists one upper-arm bone, two lower-arm bones, and five digits, so the limbs share the same bone plan even though their jobs differ. Choosing 'same job' confuses shared function with shared structure, which is the key idea being tested.

questions.stem: Select all statements that are supported by the evidence.
options: The four mammals share the same limb-bone pattern even though their limbs do different jobs.
The matching bone arrangement is evidence that the four mammals share a common ancestor.
The tiny hip bones in whales are evidence of ancestors that had hind limbs.
Because the limbs do different jobs, the four mammals cannot be related.
Each mammal built its limb bones from a completely different plan.
questions.rationale: The shared bone pattern (0) and the vestigial whale hip bones (2) are homologous evidence of common ancestry (1). Option 3 wrongly treats different function as proof of no relationship, and option 4 contradicts the identical bone counts in the table.

questions.stem: Complete the explanation of the evidence. Forelimbs that contain the same bones in the same arrangement but do different jobs are called [Drop-down 1]. This shared arrangement is best explained if the mammals inherited their limbs from [Drop-down 2]. The reduced hip bones of whales are [Drop-down 3] that point to ancestors that once had hind limbs.
dd: homologous structures | analogous structures | vestigial structures
a shared common ancestor | four unrelated ancestors | the same living species
vestigial structures | homologous limbs | brand-new structures
questions.rationale: Same structure with different function defines homologous structures, best explained by descent from a shared common ancestor; the useless whale hip bones are vestigial structures. Picking 'analogous' or 'four unrelated ancestors' describes the opposite of the pattern in the data.

questions.stem: Decide whether each statement about using these structures as evidence is True or False.
rows: Comparing the limb bones of several different mammals is a valid way to look for evidence of common ancestry.
Because a bat's wing and a whale's flipper do different jobs, their matching bones cannot count as evidence of shared ancestry.
When anatomy, the fossil record, and DNA comparisons all point to the same relationships, the evidence for common ancestry is stronger.
A vestigial hip bone that has no use in swimming provides no evidence at all about a whale's ancestors.
questions.rationale: Comparative anatomy is a valid line of evidence, and agreement among several independent lines makes the case stronger. The two false statements repeat the misconceptions that different function erases homology and that vestigial structures carry no historical information.

stimuli.title: Fossils of Walking Whales
stimuli.phenomenon: Modern whales live their whole lives in the ocean and have no back legs, yet their skeletons still contain tiny, useless hip bones. Comparisons of anatomy and DNA had already grouped whales with hoofed land mammals, which raised a question: did whales descend from four-legged land animals? Over the past century, scientists have uncovered a series of fossils in progressively younger layers of rock. The oldest fossils are of a dog-sized land animal with four full legs. Younger fossils show animals with shorter legs, wide paddle-like feet, and nostrils placed farther back on the skull. The youngest fossils are of nearly fully aquatic animals with only tiny hind legs. Together these fossils trace a gradual change from land-dwelling to ocean-dwelling forms. The table lists several of these fossils, their approximate age, and key features. In the questions that follow, you will use this fossil evidence to explain how it supports common ancestry between whales and land mammals.

figure.caption: Table 1. Several fossil forms on the line leading to modern whales, ordered by the rock layers they were found in.
rows: Short legs with large webbed feet
Small legs; swims using its tail
Near the top of the skull
No external hind legs; tiny hip bones only
Blowhole on top of the head

questions.stem: According to the table, what happens to the hind limbs as the fossils get younger?
options: They get larger and stronger.
They get smaller and eventually disappear as external limbs.
They stay exactly the same in every form.
They move to the front of the body.
questions.rationale: From Pakicetus (four full legs) to the modern whale (only tiny internal hip bones), the hind limbs shrink over time. Reading the trend as 'larger' or 'unchanged' ignores the clear reduction shown across the rows.

questions.stem: Using their approximate ages, arrange these fossil forms in order from oldest (1) to youngest.
items: Basilosaurus - tiny, non-functional hind legs (about 38 million years ago)
Pakicetus - four full walking legs (about 50 million years ago)
Rodhocetus - small legs, swims with its tail (about 47 million years ago)
Ambulocetus - short legs with large webbed feet (about 49 million years ago)
questions.rationale: Ordered by age, the sequence is Pakicetus (50), Ambulocetus (49), Rodhocetus (47), then Basilosaurus (38). This matches the gradual loss of hind limbs and the backward shift of the nostrils recorded in progressively younger rock layers.

questions.stem: Choose the word that makes each part of the explanation correct.
items: As the fossils get younger, the animals show [ more / fewer ] features suited to life in water.
The gradual change from four-legged land forms to ocean forms supports the idea that whales share a common ancestor with [ land mammals / fish ].
The tiny hip bones inside modern whales are best explained as [ leftover / newly evolved ] structures from that ancestor.
questions.rationale: Younger fossils are more water-adapted, and the whole series links whales to land-mammal ancestors, whose reduced hind limbs survive as the whale's vestigial hip bones. Choosing 'fish' or 'newly evolved' ignores the land-to-water pattern the fossils show.

questions.stem: Besides these fossils, select all additional evidence that would help support the claim that whales share a common ancestor with land mammals.
options: DNA comparisons showing whales are closely related to hoofed land mammals
Similar arrangements of limb bones in whale flippers and land-mammal legs
The order in which body structures appear in whale and land-mammal embryos
The current ocean temperature where whales live today
The number of whales counted in the ocean this year
questions.rationale: DNA sequence comparisons, comparative anatomy, and embryology are independent lines of evidence that can each test common ancestry. Ocean temperature and a population count describe present-day conditions and say nothing about ancestry.

standards.pe_text: Construct an explanation based on evidence that the process of evolution primarily results from four factors: (1) the potential for a species to increase in number, (2) the heritable genetic variation of individuals in a species due to mutation and sexual reproduction, (3) competition for limited resources, and (4) the proliferation of those organisms that are better able to survive and reproduce in the environment.

stimuli.title: Finch Beaks After a Drought
stimuli.phenomenon: On the small Galapagos island of Daphne Major, biologists have measured a population of medium ground finches for decades. These finches eat seeds, and birds with deeper, stronger beaks can crack large, hard seeds that smaller-beaked birds cannot open, while birds with smaller, shallower beaks feed faster on small, soft seeds. Beak depth varies among individuals and is inherited by offspring. In 1977 a severe drought struck the island. Few plants produced seeds, and the small, soft seeds the finches preferred nearly disappeared, leaving mostly large, hard seeds. Many finches starved that year, and only a fraction of the population survived to breed in 1978. Table 1 shows the average beak depth of the finch population before and after the drought, along with the rainfall for each year. In the questions that follow, you will use the data to explain how natural selection changed the finch population from one generation to the next.

figure.caption: Table 1. Rainfall and average finch beak depth on Daphne Major before and after the 1977 drought.
figure.source: Data: adapted from P. R. Grant and B. R. Grant, medium ground finch measurements, Daphne Major.

questions.stem: According to Table 1, how did the average beak depth of the finch population change after the 1977 drought?
options: It increased from 9.4 mm to 9.8 mm.
It decreased from 9.8 mm to 9.4 mm.
It stayed exactly the same.
It fell to zero during the drought.
questions.rationale: The 1978 population mean (9.8 mm) is greater than the 1976 mean (9.4 mm), an increase of 0.4 mm. Option 1 reverses the direction of the change.

questions.stem: Arrange the steps to show how natural selection increased the average beak depth of the finch population.
items: A drought killed most plants, so small soft seeds became scarce and mostly large, hard seeds remained.
The survivors' offspring inherited deeper beaks, so the population's average beak depth increased.
Finches in the population vary in beak depth, and this variation is passed from parents to offspring.
Birds with deeper, stronger beaks could crack the hard seeds, so they were more likely to survive and reproduce.
questions.rationale: Correct order: heritable variation already exists, the environment changes (drought removes soft seeds), the advantageous trait aids survival and reproduction, and the trait becomes more common in the next generation.

questions.stem: Suppose several wet years follow and small, soft seeds again become the most common food. Over the next generations, the average beak depth of the finches would most likely [Drop-down 1], because finches with [Drop-down 2] beaks would be better able to feed and reproduce.
dd: increase | decrease | stay exactly the same
questions.rationale: When soft seeds are abundant, a deep beak no longer provides an advantage; smaller, shallower-beaked birds feed efficiently and reproduce, so the population average shifts back downward as the selection pressure reverses.

stimuli.title: Guppy Colors and Predators
stimuli.phenomenon: Male guppies are small freshwater fish whose bodies are marked with bright orange and blue spots. The number and size of these spots is inherited, passed from fathers to sons. Bright, spotty males attract more females and father more offspring, which by itself would make each generation more colorful. But bright spots also make a male easier for predators to see. Guppies live in streams that differ in how many predators are present. In pools packed with hungry predatory fish, a flashy male is quickly spotted and eaten before it can breed. In pools with few predators, colorful males survive long enough to attract mates and reproduce. Biologists compared males from a high-predation pool and a low-predation pool in the same stream system. The graph shows the average number of bright spots per male in each pool. In the questions that follow, you will use the data to explain how predators and mates together shape the coloring of male guppies over generations.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Average number of bright spots per male guppy in a high-predation pool and a low-predation pool.
figure.title: Male Guppy Coloring in Two Pools
figure.source: Data: adapted from Endler, 1980, guppy color-pattern studies.

questions.stem: According to the graph, how does the coloring of male guppies differ between the two pools?
options: Males in the low-predation pool have more bright spots.
Males in the high-predation pool have more bright spots.
Males in both pools have the same number of spots.
Only males in the high-predation pool have spots.
questions.rationale: The low-predation pool averages about 12 spots per male versus about 5 in the high-predation pool. Options that reverse or equalize the bars misread the clear difference in the data.

questions.stem: Arrange the steps to show how a high number of predators leads to duller males over generations.
items: In pools with many predators, the brightest males are seen and eaten before they can breed.
Male guppies vary in how bright they are, and this coloring is inherited by their sons.
Over generations, the average male in a high-predation pool becomes duller.
The duller males that survive go on to attract mates and father the next generation.
questions.rationale: The chain runs: heritable variation in brightness already exists, predators remove the brightest males, the duller survivors reproduce, and the population average shifts toward duller coloring. Placing the survivors' breeding before the predation breaks the cause-and-effect order.

questions.stem: Select all statements that correctly help explain the difference between the two pools using natural selection.
options: Because spot color is inherited, males pass their coloring on to their sons.
In high-predation pools, being bright lowers a male's chance of surviving long enough to reproduce.
In low-predation pools, bright males survive and their attractiveness to females helps them father more offspring.
Individual males change their own spot color to match how many predators are nearby.
Predators have no effect on which males survive to reproduce.
questions.rationale: Heritable color (0) combined with the survival cost of brightness under predators (1) and its mating benefit when predators are scarce (2) explains the pattern through survival and reproduction. Option 3 is the misconception that individuals change inherited traits, and option 4 contradicts the data.

questions.stem: Suppose predators are removed from the high-predation pool for many generations. The average male guppy in that pool would most likely become [Drop-down 1], because without predators the [Drop-down 2] males would survive to attract mates and reproduce.
questions.rationale: Removing predators takes away the survival cost of being colorful, so the mating advantage of bright spots wins out and males grow brighter over generations. Predicting 'duller' ignores that predation, not mating, was holding brightness down.

stimuli.title: Camouflage in Stick Insects
stimuli.phenomenon: Stick insects are slow-moving plant-eaters that avoid being eaten by looking like twigs and leaves. In one population living on a green-leaved shrub, individuals come in two inherited body colors: a green form and a brown form. A young insect's color is passed down from its parents. Birds hunt the insects by sight and pick off the ones that stand out against the leaves. Against green leaves, a brown insect is easy to see, while a green insect is well hidden. Researchers followed this population on green shrubs for several generations and recorded the percentage of green and brown insects each year. Because the better-hidden insects were more likely to survive long enough to mate and lay eggs, the makeup of the population slowly changed. The graph shows the percentage of green insects over five generations. In the questions that follow, you will use the data to explain how a heritable color, predators, and reproduction together changed this insect population over time.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Percentage of green stick insects in a population living on green shrubs over five generations.
figure.title: Percentage of Green Stick Insects Over Time

questions.stem: According to the graph, how did the percentage of green stick insects change over the five generations?
options: It decreased.
It stayed the same.
It increased.
It rose and then fell.
questions.rationale: The green percentage climbs from 55% in generation 1 to 80% in generation 5, a steady increase. The other options misread a clearly rising line.

questions.stem: Choose the word that makes each statement about the change correct.
items: A stick insect's color is [ inherited / chosen ], so parents pass it to their offspring.
On green shrubs, birds more easily see and eat the [ green / brown ] form.
Because the [ green / brown ] form is better hidden, it is more likely to survive, mate, and lay eggs.
Over the generations, the population becomes more [ green / brown ].
questions.rationale: Heritable color is passed to offspring; on green shrubs the brown form is easier for birds to spot, so the hidden green form survives and reproduces more, and the population shifts greener. Choosing 'chosen' or the wrong form breaks the natural-selection logic.

questions.stem: Decide whether each statement correctly explains the change in the population.
rows: The population changed because the better-camouflaged insects survived more often and left more offspring.
The population changed because individual brown insects turned green to hide from the birds.
Body color is heritable, so the survivors passed their color to the next generation.
Birds hunting by sight act as a selection pressure on the insects' color.
questions.rationale: Differential survival and reproduction of heritable color, with birds as the selection pressure, explains the shift. The false statement is the common misconception that individuals change their own inherited color, rather than the population changing across generations.

questions.stem: Suppose a long drought turns the shrubs brown for many generations. The percentage of brown insects would most likely [Drop-down 1], because on brown shrubs the [Drop-down 2] form would be better hidden and more likely to survive and reproduce.
questions.rationale: When the background turns brown, camouflage now favors the brown form, so brown insects survive and reproduce more and their percentage rises. This reverses the earlier advantage that green insects had on green shrubs.

standards.pe_text: Apply concepts of statistics and probability to support explanations that organisms with an advantageous heritable trait tend to increase in proportion to organisms lacking this trait.

stimuli.title: Peppered Moths and Soot
stimuli.phenomenon: Peppered moths rest on tree trunks during the day, where birds hunt them by sight. The moths come in two inherited forms: a light, speckled form and a dark form. Before the 1800s, most trees in England were covered with pale lichens, and light moths were far more common. During the Industrial Revolution, soot from coal-burning factories killed the lichens and darkened tree bark in industrial regions, while forests in the countryside stayed light. Scientists surveyed peppered moths in two woodlands during the height of industrial pollution: one near a sooty industrial city and one in the clean countryside. In field experiments, birds ate more of whichever form stood out against the bark. Figure 1 shows the percentage of dark and light moths found in each woodland. In the questions that follow, you will use the data to explain how natural selection changed the proportion of each form.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Percentage of dark and light peppered moths in two woodlands during peak industrial pollution.
figure.title: Moth forms by woodland

questions.stem: In which woodland is the dark form of the moth more common, and how does this compare with the color of the bark?
options: The dark form is more common in the industrial woodland, where the bark is dark.
The dark form is more common in the countryside, where the bark is pale.
The light form is more common in the industrial woodland.
The two forms are equally common in both woodlands.
questions.rationale: Dark moths are 90% of the industrial woodland, where soot darkened the bark. Options 1 and 2 misread the chart; option 3 ignores the clear 90/10 split.

questions.stem: Select all explanations that are supported by the data and the information given.
options: In each woodland, the more common form of moth is the one that better matches the bark.
Birds acting as predators are a selection pressure on moth color.
The dark form is better hidden from birds on pale, lichen-covered bark.
Moth color is a heritable trait that affects how easily birds spot the moths.
Pollution caused each individual moth to change its color to match the bark.
questions.rationale: The form matching the bark is more common in each woodland (0), and birds selectively eating the more visible form links color to survival (1, 3). Option 2 is backward, and option 5 is the misconception that environment directly changes an individual's inherited traits.

questions.stem: In the mid-1900s, clean-air laws reduced soot, and lichens regrew so that bark in former industrial areas became pale again. Over the following decades, the proportion of dark moths in those areas would most likely [Drop-down 1], because [Drop-down 2] moths would now be better hidden from predators.
dd: light | dark | both light and dark
questions.rationale: As bark becomes pale again the selection pressure reverses: light moths are better camouflaged, survive predation, and reproduce, so the dark form declines. This directional shift back toward the light form is directional selection.

stimuli.title: Pocket Mice on Dark Lava
stimuli.phenomenon: Rock pocket mice live in the deserts of the American Southwest, where they are hunted at night by owls that find them by sight. Across most of the desert the ground is pale sandy soil, but in some places ancient lava flows have left large patches of black rock. The mice come in two inherited coat colors: a light, sandy color and a dark color. On pale desert soil a light mouse blends in while a dark mouse stands out; on black lava rock the reverse is true. Scientists trapped mice at a light-soil site and at a nearby dark-lava site and recorded the coat color of each mouse. They found that the coat color of the mice closely matched the color of the ground they lived on. The table shows the percentage of dark and light mice at each site. In the questions that follow, you will use the data to explain how predators can shape the coat color of a population.

figure.caption: Table 1. Percentage of dark-colored and light-colored pocket mice at two nearby desert sites.
figure.source: Data: adapted from rock pocket mouse studies (Nachman et al., 2003).

questions.stem: According to the table, which coat color is most common on the dark lava rock?
options: Light-colored mice
Dark-colored mice
The two colors are equally common
No mice live on lava rock
questions.rationale: On the dark lava rock, 86% of mice are dark-colored versus only 14% light. Selecting 'light' or 'equal' misreads the strong majority shown in the table.

questions.stem: Select all statements that are supported by the data and the information given.
options: At each site, the more common coat color is the one that better matches the ground.
Owls hunting by sight act as a selection pressure on coat color.
Coat color is a heritable trait that affects how easily an owl can spot a mouse.
The lava rock changed the genes of the mice so their fur turned dark.
Dark mice are more common on pale soil than on lava rock.
questions.rationale: The camouflaged color dominates at each site (0), and heritable coat color plus visual owl predation (1, 2) explains why. Option 3 is the misconception that the environment directly changes genes, and option 5 reverses the data (dark mice are 86% on lava but 5% on soil).

questions.stem: Choose the word that makes each prediction correct.
items: A light-colored mouse that wanders onto black lava rock would be [ easier / harder ] for an owl to see.
That mouse would be [ less / more ] likely to survive and reproduce than a dark mouse on the same rock.
So on lava rock, natural selection favors the [ dark / light ] coat color.
questions.rationale: A light mouse stands out on black rock, so it is easier for an owl to catch and less likely to survive and reproduce, which means selection on lava favors the dark coat. Reversing any choice ignores how camouflage affects survival.

questions.stem: Decide whether each statement correctly summarizes what the data show.
rows: On light desert soil, most mice are light-colored.
On dark lava rock, most mice are dark-colored.
The data show that coat color and the color of the ground are unrelated.
At both sites, the coat color that better hides mice from owls is the more common one.
questions.rationale: Light mice dominate the light soil (95%) and dark mice dominate the lava (86%), so coat color clearly tracks the ground color and the better-camouflaged color is more common. The false statement claims no relationship, which the matched percentages contradict.

stimuli.title: Soapberry Bugs and Their Food
stimuli.phenomenon: Soapberry bugs feed by pushing a long, thin mouthpart, called a beak, through the wall of a fruit to reach the seeds inside. In Florida, these bugs traditionally fed on a native balloon vine, which has large, round fruit with seeds set deep inside. About 50 years ago, people planted the golden rain tree, whose fruit is small and flat, so its seeds sit close to the surface. Beak length is an inherited trait that varies among bugs. On the flat introduced fruit, bugs with shorter beaks reach the seeds more easily, feed better, and leave more offspring, while a long beak is wasted effort. Scientists measured the average beak length of bugs living on each kind of fruit. Figure 1 shows the results. In the questions that follow, you will use the data to explain how an advantageous inherited trait became more common in a population.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Average beak length of soapberry bugs on each host fruit.
figure.title: Beak length differs by host fruit

questions.stem: According to Figure 1, how does the average beak length of bugs on the small, flat introduced fruit compare with that of bugs on the large native fruit?
options: It is shorter.
It is longer.
It is exactly the same.
It is zero.
questions.rationale: Bars show about 6.9 mm versus 10.2 mm, so bugs on the shallow-seed fruit have shorter beaks.

questions.stem: Select all statements that are evidence that shorter beaks are an adaptation to the small, flat fruit.
options: Beak length is inherited, so it can be passed to offspring.
On the flat fruit, shorter-beaked bugs reach the seeds more easily and feed better.
Every bug grows a shorter beak during its own life to match its fruit.
Bugs that feed better leave more offspring, so the trait becomes more common.
Beak length has nothing to do with which fruit a bug can use.
questions.rationale: A, B, D give the heritable-variation + advantage + differential-reproduction chain; C is Lamarckian (individuals do not change their own beaks) and E denies the link.

questions.stem: Arrange the steps to show how the population on the introduced fruit came to have shorter beaks.
items: Bugs with shorter beaks feed more efficiently on the flat fruit and leave more offspring.
Beak length varies among the bugs, and the trait is inherited.
Over generations, short beaks become more common in the population on the flat fruit.
Some bugs begin feeding on the small, flat introduced fruit.
questions.rationale: Variation exists (B) then bugs use the new fruit (D) then short-beaked bugs out-reproduce (A) then short beaks increase (C): B -> D -> A -> C.

questions.stem: Decide whether each statement is True or False.
rows: A trait is called an adaptation when it is inherited and helps organisms survive and reproduce in their environment.
The introduced fruit caused each individual bug to grow a shorter beak on purpose.
If the bugs returned to using only the large native fruit, longer beaks would likely become more common again.
questions.rationale: Adaptations are heritable and raise fitness; individuals do not choose to change their beaks; selection would favor longer beaks again on deep-seed fruit.

standards.pe_text: Construct an explanation based on evidence for how natural selection leads to adaptation of populations.

stimuli.title: Rise of Antibiotic Resistance
stimuli.phenomenon: When a person takes an antibiotic to treat a bacterial infection, the drug kills bacteria that are sensitive to it. However, in any large population of bacteria, a few cells carry inherited traits, such as a pump that removes the drug or an altered target the drug cannot attach to, that let them survive the antibiotic. A hospital tracked one common type of bacteria over 12 years while a particular antibiotic was used heavily to treat infections. Each year, the hospital measured the percentage of infections caused by bacteria that no longer responded to that antibiotic. Because bacteria reproduce quickly, they pass their traits to huge numbers of offspring in a short time. Figure 1 shows how the percentage of resistant infections changed over the 12 years. In the questions that follow, you will use the data to explain how natural selection led this bacterial population to become adapted to the antibiotic.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Percentage of infections resistant to the antibiotic over 12 years of heavy use.
figure.title: Resistant infections over time

questions.stem: Decide whether each statement is True or False based on the data and on how natural selection works.
rows: The percentage of infections resistant to the antibiotic increased over the 12 years.
The antibiotic caused individual bacteria to change into resistant cells so they could survive.
Resistant bacteria were already present in the population and survived to reproduce while others were killed.
Heavy use of the antibiotic gave resistant bacteria a survival advantage over non-resistant bacteria.
questions.rationale: The data rise from 5% to 62% (True). Resistance comes from pre-existing heritable variation that the drug selects for, not from the drug transforming individuals (statement 2 is the key misconception, so False; statements 3 and 4 are True).

questions.stem: Arrange the steps to show how natural selection led this bacterial population to become adapted to the antibiotic.
items: The antibiotic is used heavily and kills most of the non-resistant bacteria.
Over many generations, resistant bacteria make up a larger and larger percentage of the population.
Within the bacterial population, a few cells carry an inherited trait that lets them survive the antibiotic.
The surviving resistant bacteria reproduce rapidly, passing the trait to their offspring.
questions.rationale: Correct order: heritable variation exists first, the antibiotic kills non-resistant cells, resistant survivors reproduce and pass on the trait, and the resistant form becomes the majority over generations.

questions.stem: Suppose the hospital sharply reduces its use of this antibiotic, and being resistant carries a small energy cost. Which outcome is most likely over the next several years?
options: The percentage of resistant bacteria may level off or slowly decrease, because resistance no longer provides a strong survival advantage.
All bacteria will immediately become resistant, because the antibiotic is gone.
The bacteria will lose the ability to reproduce.
The resistant bacteria will change into a completely different species within a year.
questions.rationale: Removing the antibiotic removes the advantage of resistance; if resistance carries a cost, non-resistant cells compete better, so the resistant share levels off or declines. The other options misapply selection and confuse it with instant, guaranteed change.

stimuli.title: Beetles That Survive the Spray
stimuli.phenomenon: A beetle that feeds on potato plants can destroy an entire field if it is not controlled. For many years, farmers in one region sprayed the same insecticide on their fields to kill these beetles. When the spraying first began, almost every beetle that was exposed died. Within any large beetle population, however, a few individuals happen to carry an inherited trait that lets them break down the insecticide and survive. These survivors passed the trait to their offspring, and because the beetles produce a new generation each season, the trait spread quickly. Scientists sampled the beetle population every few generations and recorded the percentage that could survive the normal spray. Over about 25 generations, the insecticide killed fewer and fewer beetles, and farmers had to spray more and more often. Figure 1 shows how the percentage of resistant beetles changed over the generations. In the questions that follow, you will use the data to explain how natural selection led this beetle population to become adapted to the insecticide.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Percentage of a crop beetle population able to survive the normal insecticide spray, by generation.
figure.title: Resistant Beetles Over Generations

questions.stem: According to Figure 1, how did the percentage of resistant beetles change over the 25 generations?
options: It steadily decreased.
It increased over the generations.
It stayed about the same.
It increased and then returned to its starting value.
questions.rationale: The line climbs from about 4% to about 80%, so resistance rose steadily. Reading it as flat or decreasing misreads the upward trend, and it never returns to the start.

questions.stem: Complete the explanation of how the beetle population changed. Before spraying, a few beetles already carried an inherited trait that let them [Drop-down 1] the insecticide. Each time the field was sprayed, most beetles without the trait [Drop-down 2], while those with the trait survived and [Drop-down 3]. Over many generations, resistant beetles made up a larger and larger share of the population.
dd: break down and survive | be attracted to | grow larger from
passed the trait to their offspring | lost the trait | changed into a new species
correct: passed the trait to their offspring
questions.rationale: Natural selection acts on pre-existing heritable variation: the spray removes susceptible beetles, resistant survivors reproduce, and the inherited trait becomes more common. The distractors reverse the survival advantage or claim the spray created the trait.

questions.stem: Select all statements that are supported by the data and by how natural selection works.
options: Resistant beetles were present in the population before the trait became common.
Spraying the insecticide caused individual beetles to change so that they could survive it.
Beetles with the resistance trait survived spraying and left more offspring than beetles without it.
The share of resistant beetles rose because the insecticide gave resistant beetles a survival advantage.
Every beetle in the field became resistant at exactly the same time.
questions.rationale: Resistance came from variation already present, and selection favored the survivors that reproduced. The unselected options are the misconceptions that the chemical transformed individuals or that the whole population changed at once.

questions.stem: Choose the word that makes each prediction correct.
items: If the farmers keep using only this same insecticide, the percentage of resistant beetles will most likely [ rise / fall ] even further.
If the farmers switch to a very different insecticide that resistant beetles cannot survive, the percentage of beetles resistant to that new chemical would at first be [ low / high ].
Because resistance is [ inherited / learned ], it can be passed on to the next generation of beetles.
questions.rationale: Continued selection pushes resistance higher; a brand-new chemical starts with few resistant beetles because that trait is initially rare; and the trait spreads only because it is heritable, not learned.

stimuli.title: Rats That Resist the Poison
stimuli.phenomenon: For decades, people have used a poison in bait to control brown rats in cities and on farms. The poison works by stopping a rat's blood from clotting normally. When it was first introduced, a standard dose killed almost every rat that ate the bait. In a large rat population, though, a few rats carried an inherited trait that let their blood keep clotting even after they ate the poison. These rats survived, bred, and passed the trait to their pups. Because rats reproduce several times a year, the trait spread through the population over the following decades. Pest-control workers in one area recorded, every ten years, the percentage of rats that carried the resistance trait and the percentage of exposed rats that a standard dose still killed. Table 1 shows their results. In the questions that follow, you will use the data to explain how natural selection led this rat population to become adapted to the poison.

figure.caption: Table 1. Resistance in a brown rat population and the effectiveness of a standard poison dose, 1960 to 2000.
columns: Exposed rats killed by a standard dose (%)

questions.stem: According to Table 1, what happened between 1960 and 2000?
options: The percentage of resistant rats rose while the poison killed a smaller and smaller percentage of rats.
Both the percentage of resistant rats and the poison's effectiveness rose.
The percentage of resistant rats fell while the poison became more effective.
Neither value changed over the 40 years.
questions.rationale: Resistance climbs from 2% to 69% while the dose's kill rate falls from 96% to 28%. The other options reverse one or both trends shown in the table.

questions.stem: Match each observation to the part of natural selection it best illustrates.
rows: A few rats could survive the poison even before it was widely used
The poison bait killed most rats but not the ones carrying the trait
Surviving rats bred and passed the trait to their pups
After many generations, most rats in the area were resistant
questions.optset: heritable variation / selection pressure / differential survival and reproduction / adaptation of the population
questions.rationale: Pre-existing survivors show heritable variation, the poison is the selection pressure, resistant rats out-survive and out-reproduce others, and the population as a whole becomes adapted. Mismatches reveal confusion about which step each observation represents.

questions.stem: Decide whether each statement is True or False based on the data and on how natural selection works.
rows: The rise in resistance is evidence that the poison selected for rats that already carried the resistance trait.
The poison caused each rat's body to build resistance so that it would not die.
As resistant rats became common, the same dose of poison killed a smaller share of the rats.
The resistance trait is passed from parent rats to their offspring.
questions.rationale: Selection acted on variation already present, so statement 1 is true, and the false statement 2 is the key misconception that the poison transformed individuals. The falling kill rate and the inheritance of the trait make statements 3 and 4 true.

questions.stem: Predict what would happen next. Suppose pest-control workers switch to a new poison that works in a completely different way, and the resistant rats have no trait that protects them from it. At first, the new poison would kill [Drop-down 1] of the rats. If this new poison is then used heavily for many years, natural selection could cause resistance to the new poison to [Drop-down 2].
dd: increase over generations | disappear immediately | stay at zero forever
questions.rationale: Because the old trait gives no protection against a different poison, most rats die at first; but heavy use of the new poison would again select for any rats that can survive it, so resistance to it could rise over generations. The distractors ignore how selection repeats whenever a new pressure is applied.

standards.pe_text: Evaluate the evidence supporting claims that changes in environmental conditions may result in: (1) increases in the number of individuals of some species, (2) the emergence of new species over time, and (3) the extinction of other species.

stimuli.title: Change Comes to Lake Victoria
stimuli.phenomenon: Lake Victoria in East Africa once held more than 500 species of small, colorful fish called cichlids. All of these species arose from a few ancestors over a relatively short time, a burst of new species known as an adaptive radiation, each adapted to a different food or habitat in the lake. In the 1950s, people introduced the Nile perch, a large predatory fish, to boost fishing catches. Around the same time, fertilizer runoff from farms fed huge blooms of algae that clouded the water. Cichlids find mates partly by color, which they could no longer see clearly in the murky water. Table 1 shows how the number of native cichlid species, the Nile perch catch, and the water clarity changed over 30 years. In the questions that follow, you will use the data to evaluate how a change in the environment affected different species in the lake.

figure.caption: Table 1. Native cichlid species, Nile perch catch, and water clarity in Lake Victoria, 1970 to 2000.

questions.stem: According to Table 1, what happened as water clarity decreased from 1970 to 2000?
options: The number of native cichlid species decreased while the Nile perch catch increased.
Both the number of cichlid species and the Nile perch catch increased.
The number of cichlid species increased while the Nile perch catch decreased.
Nothing changed except the water clarity.
questions.rationale: Cichlid species fall from 120 to 28 while the perch catch rises from 1,000 to 150,000 tonnes. The other options misread one or both trends.

questions.stem: This example shows that changes in the environment can have several different effects on species. The large rise in the Nile perch is an example of [Drop-down 1]. The loss of most native cichlid species is an example of [Drop-down 2]. The earlier formation of hundreds of cichlid species from a few ancestors is an example of [Drop-down 3].
dd: an increase in the number of individuals of a species | the extinction of species | the emergence of new species
an increase in the number of individuals of a species | the extinction of species | the emergence of new species
