an increase in the number of individuals of a species | the extinction of species | the emergence of new species
correct: an increase in the number of individuals of a species
questions.rationale: The three outcomes of environmental change map to the data: the perch population grew (increase), most cichlids disappeared (extinction), and the earlier adaptive radiation produced many new species (emergence).

questions.stem: Decide whether each statement is supported (True) or not supported (False) by the data.
rows: The decline in native cichlid species happened at the same time as the rise in Nile perch and the drop in water clarity.
The data show that the environmental change caused every species in the lake to go extinct.
An environmental change can cause some species to increase in number while others decline.
The Nile perch catch stayed constant throughout the 30 years.
questions.rationale: The three trends move together over the same years (True). Not every species went extinct because the Nile perch increased (statement 2 False), which also shows different species can respond in opposite directions (statement 3 True); the perch catch clearly changed (statement 4 False).

stimuli.title: After the Asteroid
stimuli.phenomenon: About 66 million years ago, a mountain-sized asteroid struck the Earth. The impact threw enormous amounts of dust and rock into the sky, blocking sunlight around the world for months to years. With little sunlight reaching the surface, many plants and the tiny ocean producers that depend on light died back sharply. This sudden environmental change rippled through food webs everywhere. Large animals that needed a great deal of food, including the non-avian dinosaurs, disappeared, and ammonites, a group of shelled ocean animals, vanished as well. Not every group died out. Some small mammals and the ancestors of modern birds survived the crisis, probably because they could live on seeds, insects, and other scraps. In the millions of years that followed, these survivors spread into habitats left empty by the extinctions and gave rise to many new species. Figure 1 compares the variety of four groups before the impact and after the recovery. In the questions that follow, you will use the evidence to evaluate how a sudden environmental change affected different groups of living things.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Relative variety of four groups before the asteroid impact and after the recovery that followed.
figure.title: Variety of Four Groups Before and After the Impact

questions.stem: According to Figure 1, which two groups had a variety of about zero after the recovery?
options: Ammonites and non-avian dinosaurs
Mammals and birds
Ammonites and mammals
Non-avian dinosaurs and birds
questions.rationale: The bars for ammonites and non-avian dinosaurs fall to about zero after the recovery, meaning these groups died out. Mammals and birds instead rise, so any option pairing them with the extinct groups misreads the chart.

questions.stem: Match each group to what happened to it across the impact, based on Figure 1.
questions.optset: died out (extinction) / survived and increased in variety
questions.rationale: Ammonites and non-avian dinosaurs dropped to about zero (extinction), while mammals and birds rose to a greater variety than before (survived and diversified). Sorting them the other way ignores the direction of each pair of bars.

questions.stem: Complete the cause-and-effect explanation. The impact filled the sky with dust, which [Drop-down 1] the amount of sunlight reaching the surface. With less sunlight, many [Drop-down 2] died back, so large animals that needed a lot of food [Drop-down 3]. Small survivors that could eat seeds and insects later spread and gave rise to [Drop-down 4].
dd: producers such as plants and ocean algae | large predators | shelled ocean animals
ran short of food and went extinct | grew much larger | were unaffected
many new species | no new species | identical copies of themselves
correct: producers such as plants and ocean algae
ran short of food and went extinct
questions.rationale: Blocking sunlight cut off the producers at the base of food webs, starving large consumers into extinction, while surviving small animals later diversified into many new species. This chain links the three outcomes of environmental change: extinction, increase, and emergence.

questions.stem: A scientist claims that the asteroid impact caused these extinctions. Select all of the additional pieces of evidence that would best support this claim.
options: A worldwide layer of rock, dated to the same time, that contains material common in asteroids.
Dinosaur fossils that are common just below that rock layer but are absent above it.
Many new kinds of mammal fossils that first appear just above that rock layer.
Reports that non-avian dinosaurs are still commonly found alive in remote forests today.
Rock layers showing that ammonite shells have become more common over the last hundred years.
questions.rationale: A global impact layer, dinosaurs vanishing at that layer, and mammals diversifying just above it all tie the extinctions and later diversification to the impact. The unselected options contradict the well-supported fact that these groups are extinct.

stimuli.title: A Lake Grows Warmer
stimuli.phenomenon: A deep freshwater lake has slowly warmed over the past 50 years as the regional climate has changed. Biologists have surveyed the lake's fish every decade. When the surveys began, the lake was cold and clear and was dominated by a native whitefish that thrives in cold water. As the surface water warmed, the whitefish became harder and harder to find, while a warm-water sunfish that had once been rare began to multiply. The warming also lowered the oxygen in the deep water. Over time, a distinct form of the whitefish appeared in the deepest, coolest part of the lake; it is smaller and feeds differently, and biologists think it is slowly diverging from the original whitefish as it becomes suited to the changed conditions. Figure 1 shows how the numbers of these fish changed as the lake warmed. In the questions that follow, you will use the evidence to evaluate how a changing environment can cause some species to increase, others to decline, and new forms to appear.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Numbers of three kinds of fish caught in standard surveys as the lake warmed, 1975 to 2025.
figure.title: Fish Numbers as the Lake Warmed

questions.stem: According to Figure 1, how did the numbers of the cold-water whitefish and the warm-water sunfish change from 1975 to 2025?
options: The whitefish decreased while the sunfish increased.
Both the whitefish and the sunfish increased.
The whitefish increased while the sunfish decreased.
Both stayed about the same.
questions.rationale: The whitefish line falls from about 520 to 40 while the sunfish line rises from about 30 to 560. The other options misread one or both trends.

questions.stem: Arrange the events in the order that best shows the cause-and-effect chain in the lake, from first to last.
items: The cold-water whitefish declines while the warm-water sunfish increases.
A new deep-water form of the whitefish appears and begins to diverge.
The lake's water warms and its deep water loses oxygen.
The changed conditions favor warm-water fish and disfavor cold-water fish.
questions.rationale: The warming and oxygen loss come first, they change which fish are favored, the populations shift in response, and only later does a new form emerge. Placing the population changes before the warming breaks the cause-and-effect logic.

questions.stem: Select all of the inferences that are supported by the data in Figure 1.
options: The environmental change increased the number of one kind of fish while decreasing the number of another.
A new form of fish appeared during the same period in which the lake warmed.
The warming caused every kind of fish in the lake to disappear.
The changing environment affected different fish in different ways.
The warm-water sunfish went extinct in the lake.
questions.rationale: The data show one kind rising, another falling, and a new form emerging, so the change had several different effects. The unselected options are contradicted by the data, since not all fish disappeared and the sunfish clearly increased.

questions.stem: Choose the word or phrase that makes each part of the explanation correct.
items: As the lake warmed, the cold-water whitefish [ declined / increased ] because the water became less suited to it.
The same warming [ helped / harmed ] the warm-water sunfish, whose numbers rose.
The appearance of a distinct deep-water form is an example of the [ emergence of a new kind of organism / immediate extinction of all fish ].
Together these changes show that a single environmental change can [ have several different effects / have only one effect ] on the species in a community.
correct: emergence of a new kind of organism
questions.rationale: Warming disfavored the cold-water fish, favored the warm-water fish, and set the stage for a new form to emerge, so one change produced increase, decline, and emergence together. Choosing the opposite words would contradict the trends in the data.

standards.pe_text: Create or revise a simulation to test a solution to mitigate adverse impacts of human activity on biodiversity.

stimuli.title: Testing Solutions for a River Fish
stimuli.phenomenon: A native migratory fish in a large river has declined sharply. Two human activities are responsible: a dam blocks the fish from swimming upstream to their spawning grounds, and heavy commercial fishing (overexploitation) removes many adults before they reproduce. Conservation scientists built a computer simulation of the river to test possible solutions before spending money on them. The simulation models how the fish population would respond over 20 years to different actions, and it also estimates the relative cost of each action. The options compared were: taking no action (a baseline for comparison); setting a catch limit on fishing; building a fish ladder that lets fish swim past the dam; and combining a catch limit with a fish ladder. Table 1 shows the population the simulation projects after 20 years, and the relative cost, for each solution. In the questions that follow, you will use the simulation's results to evaluate which solution best protects this species.

figure.caption: Table 1. Simulated fish population after 20 years and relative cost for each tested solution.

questions.stem: Based on the simulation results in Table 1, which solution is projected to produce the largest fish population after 20 years?
options: No action
Catch limit only
Fish ladder only
Catch limit + fish ladder
questions.rationale: The combined solution reaches 41 thousand, the largest projected population in the simulator's output. Each single action (18 or 22 thousand) yields fewer fish, and no action leaves only 5 thousand.

questions.stem: Select all statements that are supported by the simulation data.
options: Every option that reduces fishing or restores fish passage is projected to produce a larger population than taking no action.
Combining a catch limit with a fish ladder is projected to more than double the population reached by a catch limit alone.
Building a fish ladder alone is projected to produce a smaller population than taking no action.
A catch limit alone is projected to produce a larger population than the combined solution.
Addressing both human activities together is projected to protect the species better than addressing either one alone.
questions.rationale: 18, 22, and 41 all exceed the no-action value of 5 (0); 41 is more than double 18 (1); and 41 tops both single actions (4). Options 2 and 3 reverse the comparisons shown in the table.

questions.stem: Choose the word or phrase that makes each statement about the trade-offs correct.
items: Every solution that lowers fishing pressure or restores fish passage [ increases / decreases ] the projected population compared with no action.
The fish ladder alone reaches a larger population than a catch limit alone, but at a [ higher / lower ] cost.
The combined solution gives the best protection for the species but is [ more / less ] expensive than a catch limit alone.
If cost must be kept low, the [ catch limit only / combined ] solution is the better cost-benefit choice.
questions.rationale: Reducing overexploitation or restoring passage raises the projected population; the fish ladder is more effective than a catch limit but costs more; the combined solution is most effective yet most costly; so under a low-cost constraint the catch limit gives the best cost-benefit balance.

stimuli.title: Reconnecting the Mountain Lions
stimuli.phenomenon: A busy highway cuts through the range of a population of mountain lions, splitting their habitat into two pieces. The lions rarely cross the highway safely, so the two groups almost never meet. Over time, each isolated group has fewer mates to choose from, and its genetic variation is shrinking, which can make the population less healthy. Conservation planners want to reconnect the habitat by building wildlife crossings, such as overpasses planted with vegetation, so the lions can move between the two sides. Before committing money, the planners built a computer simulation of the population. The simulation projects the mountain lion population and its genetic diversity 25 years into the future under different strategies, and it estimates the relative cost of each. The strategies compared are taking no action, building one overpass, building two overpasses with fencing to guide the lions, and adding habitat protection on top of the two overpasses. Table 1 shows the simulation's results. In the questions that follow, you will use the simulation to evaluate which strategy best protects this population.

figure.caption: Table 1. Simulated mountain lion population and genetic diversity after 25 years, with relative cost, for each strategy.

questions.stem: Based on Table 1, which strategy is projected to produce the largest mountain lion population after 25 years?
options: No action
One overpass
Two overpasses + fencing
Two overpasses + fencing + habitat protection
questions.rationale: The most complete strategy reaches 72 lions, the highest projected population in the simulation. Each smaller strategy yields fewer lions, and no action leaves only 15.

questions.stem: Use the data to compare two strategies. The 'two overpasses + fencing' strategy is projected to support about [Drop-down 1] the population of the no-action strategy, but it also carries a [Drop-down 2] cost.
questions.rationale: 58 lions is close to four times the 15 lions projected with no action, and the table lists that strategy's cost as high. This captures the trade-off between a large benefit and a high cost.

questions.stem: Match each strategy to the level of genetic diversity the simulation projects for it.
questions.optset: lowest / middle / highest
questions.rationale: The diversity index rises from 0.30 (no action) to 0.44 (one overpass) to 0.67 (the fullest strategy), showing that reconnecting the habitat lets the two groups mix and preserves more genetic variation. Reversing the order ignores this pattern.

questions.stem: The planners will use the simulation to choose a strategy. Select all conclusions that the simulation's results support.
options: Every strategy that adds a crossing is projected to produce a larger population than taking no action.
Reconnecting the habitat is projected to raise the population's genetic diversity above the no-action level.
Building one overpass is projected to protect the population better than two overpasses plus habitat protection.
If the very highest cost cannot be afforded, 'two overpasses + fencing' still greatly improves the population over no action.
Taking no action is projected to give the healthiest population.
questions.rationale: Every crossing strategy beats no action for both population and diversity, and a lower-cost option still helps a great deal, which supports proposing it if budget is limited. The unselected options reverse the ranking shown by the simulator.

stimuli.title: Saving an Island Bird
stimuli.phenomenon: A flightless parrot lives on a single island and nowhere else. Rats and cats brought to the island by ships eat the parrots' eggs and chicks, and much of the birds' forest habitat has been cleared for farming. Fewer than a hundred parrots remain, so the species is critically endangered. Conservation biologists are considering a rescue plan with two parts: protecting and replanting the forest habitat, and running a captive-breeding program in which parrots are raised safely and then released into the wild. Building the plan is expensive, so the biologists created a computer simulation to test it first. The simulation projects the wild parrot population over the next 30 years under four strategies: taking no action, protecting habitat only, captive breeding and release only, and combining habitat protection with captive breeding and release. Figure 1 shows the projected population for each strategy. In the questions that follow, you will use the simulation to evaluate which strategy best protects this species and how it might be improved.

figure.caption: Figure 1. Simulated wild population of the island parrot over 30 years under four strategies.
figure.title: Projected Wild Population Under Four Strategies

questions.stem: According to Figure 1, which strategy is projected to give the largest wild parrot population after 30 years?
options: No action
Habitat protection only
Captive breeding and release only
Habitat protection + captive breeding
questions.rationale: The combined strategy reaches about 355 parrots at year 30, the highest of the four lines. Each single action ends lower (about 190 or 205), and no action falls to about 15.

questions.stem: Choose the word or phrase that makes each statement correct, based on Figure 1.
items: With no action, the projected parrot population [ rises / falls ] over the 30 years.
Captive breeding and release alone raises the population, but without enough protected habitat its numbers eventually [ level off / keep climbing steeply ].
Combining habitat protection with captive breeding protects the population [ better than / worse than ] either action used alone.
questions.rationale: No action lets the population collapse, releasing birds without habitat only helps until numbers plateau, and the two actions together outperform either one, because more habitat lets released birds survive and breed. The opposite choices contradict the shapes of the lines.

questions.stem: A team must choose a strategy using a limited budget. Decide whether each statement about judging the strategies is True or False.
rows: A useful criterion for judging a strategy is how large a wild population it is projected to sustain.
Cost is not a real constraint, because the most expensive strategy is always the right choice.
If money is very limited, protecting habitat only still keeps the population from collapsing, unlike taking no action.
Taking no action meets the goal of protecting the species.
questions.rationale: Projected population size is a sensible criterion, and cost really does constrain the choice, so the most expensive option is not automatically best. Habitat protection alone still prevents collapse, while no action lets the population fall and fails the goal.

questions.stem: The team will use the simulation to guide its decision. Select all statements that the simulation's results support.
options: Combining habitat protection with captive breeding and release is projected to protect the species best.
Releasing captive-bred parrots without protecting habitat is projected to help at first but then level off.
The simulation could be improved by also testing a strategy that removes the rats and cats that eat the eggs and chicks.
Because no action lets the population fall, it is the best way to save both money and the species.
Every strategy is projected to produce the same population after 30 years.
questions.rationale: The combined strategy is projected to work best, releases alone plateau without habitat, and adding a predator-removal option is a reasonable modification to test next. The unselected options contradict the simulator, which shows no action failing and the four strategies ending at very different populations.
